objectives: Say what Allah created Adam from and what the chapter says about the human’s future on earth.
Put the opening events in order and explain the chapter’s link: Soil from different parts of the earth → different skin colors.
Look at past forms (said, began, got, created), tell a finished event (collected, shaped) from a plan told in the past (was going to create), and use because / After that / Because of this.
Talk about human difference with respectful, non-ranking words.
content.pedagogy: Start with the story, not with a rule. Learners listen with books closed, then put event strips in order and read them aloud. Only then do they look at the verbs: one question — “Did this happen, or was it a plan for later?” — lets them sort collected / shaped / was going to create before you name the forms. The skin-color sentence becomes a short, calm D14 Respect moment: People are different, and no color is better.
priorKnowledge: Common past forms (went, said) and simple sequence words (first, then).
anticipatedMisconceptions: Adam was created from soil; fire belongs to Iblis in Chapter 3.
The skin-color sentence describes difference; it does not rank people.
“Was going to” here is a plan, not movement to a place.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: past forms (say → said, begin → began, get → got, create → created) · finished event vs plan told in the past (collected, shaped / was going to create) · because (reason), After that (next step), Because of this (result).
Notice (Activity 1): board “Angels got surprised. They began waiting with curiosity.” Ask: “Is this now or a long time ago? How do you know?” Pairs match the four verbs and say which one adds -ed and which ones change.
Build (Activities 2–3): Choose collected / was going to / shaped, asking each time “Did it happen, or was it a plan for later?”, then complete because / After that / Because of this and say which word gives a reason, which the next step and which a result.
Likely errors: *sayed, *beginned · *he were going to · After that used for a reason · *Because this.
Use (Activity 4): pairs retell the opening in three or four sentences with past forms, one “was going to” and two linking words.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Chunk the plan sentence: “After THAT, | he told the AN-gels | that he was going to cre-ATE a HU-man.” “was” and “to” are weak (/wəz/, /tə/).
-ed endings: created /ɪd/, collected /ɪd/, cared /d/, surprised /d/, shaped /t/.
The color list rises on each item and falls on the last: “white↗, red↗, black↗, and YEL-low↘”.
Word focus: MES-sen-ger, cu-ri-OS-i-ty, GRAND-chil-dren, fan-TAS-tic, sur-PRISED.
beforeReading: Show a little soil in a jar or a photo of soil in different colors. Ask: “What can grow in soil? What could Allah create from it?” Keep one prediction on the board.
duringReading: First listening, books closed: What did Allah create first, and what did He shape Adam from?
Read along and underline every past verb in paragraph 2.
Box the plan sentence: “He told the angels that He was going to create a human.”
Draw an arrow from “soil from different parts of the earth” to “different skin colors”.
afterReading: Quick Challenge: Choose why the chapter says people have different skin colors and point to the sentence.
Language Focus: Look at the past forms (Activity 1), then practise past event vs plan and the three linking words (Activities 2–3).
Use: Retell the opening in three or four sentences, then say one respectful sentence about people being different.
content.lessonPlan: 0–4 Hook: soil jar or photo, learners say what grows in soil and predict what Allah will create from it; 4–12 Listen with books closed (What did Allah create? What did He shape Adam from?), then listen again and read along; 12–18 Event strips in pairs: Order six strips written on the board (sky and earth / told the angels / angels waited with curiosity / angels collected soil / Allah shaped Adam / different skin colors) and read them aloud in order; 18–22 Quick Challenge individually, learners show the sentence that proves the answer; 22–31 Language Focus: Activity 1 as a whole-class look (now or long ago? which verbs change?), Activities 2–3 in pairs with the question “happened or plan for later?”; 31–37 Use: Pairs retell from the strips with After that / Because of this, then each learner says one respectful sentence about difference (People are different, and …); 37–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: What did Allah say about the human’s future on earth?
Why were the angels waiting with curiosity?
Which two sentences make the soil → skin-color link?
How can we talk about different skin colors without saying one is better?
interactiveTips: Use the Soil hotspot to confirm what Adam was created from and the Earth hotspot for “Allah created the sky and the earth”.
Replay the sentence “After that, he told the angels …” and ask learners to raise a hand when they hear “was going to”.
Let weaker readers follow the highlighted text while the color list is read.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give a four-line frame and let learners say it before writing: “Allah created ____. After that, He told the angels that He was going to ____. The angels collected ____. Because of this, ____.”
differentiation.fastFinishers: Retell five events with three different past forms, one “was going to” and three linking words, then add one sentence about respecting difference.

formativeAssessment: Orders the opening events correctly.
Tells a finished event from a plan (collected vs was going to create).
Uses because / After that / Because of this for reason, next step and result.
expectedResponses: Allah created Adam from soil.
He told the angels that he was going to create a human.
The angels collected soil from different parts of the earth. Because of this, humans have different skin colors.
content.transferTask: Say one respectful sentence about people in your class or town being different, without saying one group is better.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners work out “happened vs plan for later” from the sentences before I named “was going to”, and did the talk about difference stay respectful?

classroomManagement.instructions: Work with your partner. Put the six strips in order from the story. Then read them aloud, one strip each.
checkQuestions: Do you write new sentences or only put the strips in order? (only put them in order)
Who reads the strips? (we take turns)
classroomManagement.monitoring: Stand at the back and listen for the strip “angels collected soil” coming before “Allah shaped Adam”. If a pair has the plan sentence (was going to create) at the end, ask “Did this happen, or was it a plan?” and move on.

exitTicket: Write two sentences about the chapter: One with “After that” and one with “Because of this”.

rubricLevels.secure: Strips match the story order with no help.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give the first and last strip and let the pair place the middle four.

rubricLevels.secure: Says collected and shaped happened, and was going to create was a plan.
rubricLevels.notYet: Point to “was going to” and ask “Before or after Allah made Adam?”.

rubricLevels.secure: Uses After that for the next step and Because of this for the result.
rubricLevels.notYet: Write the two words on two cards and let the pair hold up the right card for each strip.

rubricLevels.secure: Says one sentence about difference without “better”.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give the frame “People are different, and …” and accept one word to finish it.

interculturalFocus.notice: The chapter says soil from different parts of the earth gave people different skin colors. Difference is explained, not ranked.
interculturalFocus.compare: Ask: How many different home towns, accents or family languages are there in our class? Which English words describe people without judging them (tall, from Konya, speaks Kurdish) and which words judge?
interculturalFocus.perspective: Learners say one sentence about a classmate's background that the classmate is happy to hear. If a learner is uncomfortable sharing, they can talk about a famous person instead.

objectives: Explain what Adam could do and why he was wiser, using the chapter’s reason.
Compare the angels’ view of Adam with Iblis’s view, with one sentence from the text for each.
Look at could for past ability, compare with wiser than / more than, use taught + person + to, and report an opinion with thought + sentence.
Show respect in a disagreement through one observable action.
content.pedagogy: Put two headings on the board: “The angels” / “Iblis”. Learners find one sentence for each before anyone compares. Grammar starts from meaning: For “Adam could learn and understand” you ask “Now or in the past? Was he able or not able?” and learners answer before you name could. The thought-sentences then show two different opinions, and “But Iblis didn’t think so” is the turning point of the chapter.
priorKnowledge: Chapter 1: Allah created Adam from soil and told the angels about His plan.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Adam was wiser because Allah gave him knowledge and taught him to think, not because of what he was made from.
“Iblis thought Adam was an unimportant creature” is Iblis’s opinion, not the chapter’s view.
Naming “respect” without an action that shows it.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: could + verb = was able to (past) · comparing two: Wiser than, learned more than · taught + person + to + verb · thought (that) + sentence for an opinion · But … didn’t think so.
Notice (Activity 1): Read “Adam could learn and understand.” Ask: “Now or in the past? Was Adam able to do it?” Learners decide true/false and say the rule in their own words (could = was able to).
Build (Activities 2–3): Complete “He was wiser than the angels … taught him to think. He learned more than …” and ask “Why not wisest?”, then build “Iblis thought Adam was an unimportant creature created from clay.”
Likely errors: *could to learn · *more wiser · *wisest than · *taught him think · *Iblis think Adam was ….
Use (Activity 4): three or four sentences: What Adam could do, why he was wiser, what the angels thought and what Iblis thought.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Weak “could” (/kəd/) linked to the verb: “Adam could LEARN | and un-der-STAND”.
Contrastive stress: “ALL the AN-gels thought … | but IB-lis DIDn’t think SO”.
/θ/ in thought, think, think so: tongue between the teeth, not /t/ or /s/.
“than” is weak (/ðən/): “WIS-er than the AN-gels”.
Word focus: KNOWL-edge (silent k), re-SPECT, ad-MIRED, a-MAZ-ing, CREA-ture, un-im-POR-tant.
beforeReading: Ask: “What helps a person learn?” Pairs list three things (a teacher, books, thinking, questions). Keep the list to check against the chapter.
duringReading: Listen once: Who respected Adam and who did not?
Underline what Adam could do and the reason he was wiser (because …).
Two colors: What the angels thought / what Iblis thought.
Circle the turning word “But”.
afterReading: Quick Challenge: Choose why Adam knew more than the angels and point to the sentence with “because”.
Language Focus: Look at could (Activity 1), practise the comparisons and taught him to (Activity 2), build Iblis’s opinion sentence (Activity 3).
Use: Explain the two views in three or four sentences.
content.lessonPlan: 0–4 Hook: “What helps a person learn?” pairs list three things for a later check; 4–11 Listen once for who respected Adam and who did not, then read along; 11–18 T-chart in pairs: The angels / Iblis, one quoted sentence under each, plus the reason Adam was wiser (because …), quick board check; 18–22 Quick Challenge; 22–31 Language Focus: Activity 1 as a whole-class look (now or past? able or not?), Activity 2 in pairs (why not “wisest”?), Activity 3 individually; 31–37 Use: “Two views” in pairs, A says what the angels thought, B answers with “But Iblis thought …”, then they swap and each adds one sentence about what Adam could do; 37–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: What could Adam do, and who taught him to think?
What did the angels think about Adam? What did Iblis think?
What does “But Iblis didn’t think so” tell us?
How can we show respect to someone when we think differently?
interactiveTips: Use the Knowledge hotspot for the reason (Allah gave Adam knowledge and taught him to think) and the Angels hotspot for their admiration and respect.
Replay “All the angels thought that Adam was amazing … But Iblis didn’t think so.” and ask learners to clap once at “But”.
Read Allah’s words to the angels as they are; do not gap or change them.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Frames: “Adam could ____.” “He was wiser than ____ because ____.” “The angels thought ____. But Iblis thought ____.”
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write five sentences comparing the two views with could, wiser than, more than, taught … to and but.

formativeAssessment: Uses could for past ability.
Compares with -er than / more than (not “wisest than”).
Reports two different opinions with thought + sentence.
expectedResponses: Adam could learn and understand.
He was wiser than the angels because Allah gave Adam knowledge and taught him to think.
The angels thought Adam was amazing, but Iblis thought Adam was an unimportant creature created from clay.
content.transferTask: Give one school example of showing respect to someone you disagree with (for example: I listen first, then I say my idea politely).
content.teacherReflection: Did learners work out the meaning of could and thought from the sentences before I named them, and did they keep the two views apart?

classroomManagement.instructions: Draw a T-chart with your partner. Write “The angels” on the left and “Iblis” on the right. Copy one sentence from the story under each name.
checkQuestions: How many sentences do you copy? (two, one under each name)
Do you use your own words or the story’s words? (the story’s words)
classroomManagement.monitoring: Check that the Iblis column has “thought Adam was an unimportant creature”, not an opinion the learners made up. Listen in the Use task for “wiser than”. If you hear “wisest than”, write both forms on the board for the whole class after the task.

exitTicket: Complete: “The angels thought ____, but Iblis thought ____.”

rubricLevels.secure: Quotes one sentence for the angels and one for Iblis.
rubricLevels.notYet: Show the paragraph where each sentence is and let the learner underline it.

rubricLevels.secure: Says “Adam could learn” and “wiser than the angels” correctly.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give a choice: “wiser / wisest than” and ask which one compares two.

rubricLevels.secure: Uses “thought + sentence” for both views.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give the frame “The angels thought …, but Iblis thought …”.

rubricLevels.secure: Says one way people show respect at school.
rubricLevels.notYet: Ask “What do you do when your teacher speaks?” and accept a short answer.

interculturalFocus.notice: Adam learns the names of things, and names change across languages: Turkish Havva is Eve in English. The angels show Adam respect, and every culture has its own signs of respect.
interculturalFocus.compare: Ask: How do people show respect to an older person in Türkiye (standing up, kissing the hand, letting them sit first)? How do people show it in an English-speaking country (a handshake, Mr/Mrs, holding the door)?
interculturalFocus.perspective: Make clear that a different way of showing respect is not less respect. Learners name one sign of respect they would use with a visitor from another country.

objectives: Say what Iblis claimed about himself and why (fire and soil).
Separate what Iblis thought from what the chapter says is true about useful knowledge.
Look at thought / believed / saying as signals of someone’s idea, compare with better and more valuable, say what Iblis couldn’t see, and join ideas with But and because.
Give one example of using knowledge to do good.
content.pedagogy: The key move is two columns on the board: “Iblis’s idea” and “What the chapter says is true”. Learners sort chapter sentences into the columns and then discover that thought, believed and saying are the clue: They show an idea, not a fact. The comparatives (better, more valuable) are practised inside these real claims, so learners see the chapter’s answer: not fire, not soil, but useful knowledge makes people great.
priorKnowledge: Chapters 1–2: Adam was created from soil, Allah gave him knowledge, Iblis thought he was unimportant.
anticipatedMisconceptions: “I am better than Adam” is Iblis’s claim, not the chapter’s conclusion.
The lesson is not “fire against soil”: the chapter says the clay or the fire did not make anybody valuable.
“He thought little” means he did not think carefully.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: idea signals (thought, believed, continued saying) vs what the chapter says is true · good → better, valuable → more valuable · couldn’t + verb (was not able to) · But (a different idea) and because (a reason).
Notice (Activity 1): learners sort five parts into “What Iblis thought” / “What the chapter says is true”. Ask: “Which small word tells you it is only Iblis’s idea?” (thought, believed, saying).
Build (Activities 2–3): Choose better / more valuable / couldn’t and ask “Why not gooder? Why more with valuable?”, then complete “But useful knowledge makes people great because …”.
Likely errors: *gooder, *more better · *valuabler · *didn’t could · because used instead of But for a different idea.
Use (Activity 4): three or four sentences: What Iblis believed, one comparison, what the chapter says and a reason with because.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Report Iblis’s idea with a short pause after the verb: “He be-LIEVED | his OR-i-gin was BET-ter.”
-ed endings: believed /d/, continued /d/, created /ɪd/.
Contrast with stress: “the CLAY or the FIRE did NOT make anybody VAL-u-a-ble. | But USE-ful KNOWL-edge makes people GREAT”.
Word focus: AR-ro-gant, VAL-u-a-ble, OR-i-gin, CREA-ture, PAR-a-dise.
beforeReading: Write “fire” and “soil” on the board. Ask: “Can fire or soil make a person important? What makes a person valuable?” Collect answers as predictions and check them after reading.
duringReading: Listen once: What did Iblis say about himself?
Mark Iblis’s claim in one color and the chapter’s message about useful knowledge in another.
Find what useful knowledge helps humans do (do good and stop bad).
Underline the last sentence: Where is Adam now?
afterReading: Quick Challenge: Match Iblis, Adam, “clay or fire” and useful knowledge with what the chapter says about each.
Language Focus: Sort idea vs truth (Activity 1), practise better / more valuable / couldn’t (Activity 2) and But / because (Activity 3).
Use: Explain the wrong judgement in three or four sentences.
content.lessonPlan: 0–4 Predict: “fire” and “soil” on the board, learners say what makes a person valuable; 4–11 Listen for what Iblis said about himself, then read along; 11–19 Two-column sort in pairs: Six chapter sentences written on the board go into “Iblis’s idea” or “What the chapter says is true”, then a whole-class check where learners name the clue word; 19–23 Quick Challenge; 23–31 Language Focus: Activity 1 confirms the sort, Activities 2–3 in pairs (why better? why more valuable?); 31–37 Use: “Knowledge helps” chain, each pair writes one sentence “With knowledge, we can …” about school or home and reads it, the class adds a reason with “because …”; 37–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why did Iblis say he was better than Adam?
What was Iblis wrong about?
What does the chapter say makes people great?
How can knowledge help people do good at school?
interactiveTips: Use the Fire and Soil hotspot for the two origins and the Arrogance hotspot for Iblis’s attitude.
Replay the paragraph beginning “For Allah, …” and ask learners to raise a hand at “But”.
Read Allah’s words to Iblis calmly as they are; do not act them out.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Two columns with frames: “Iblis thought he was ____ than Adam.” / “The chapter says useful knowledge ____ because ____.”
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write four sentences contrasting Iblis’s idea with the chapter’s message, using believed, more … than, couldn’t, but and because.

formativeAssessment: Separates Iblis’s idea from the chapter’s message and names the signal word.
Uses better / more valuable correctly.
Uses But for a different idea and because for a reason.
expectedResponses: Iblis believed his origin was better because he came from the fire.
He couldn’t see that Adam had perfect knowledge.
The clay or the fire did not make anybody valuable. But useful knowledge makes people great because with this knowledge, humans can do good and stop bad.
content.transferTask: Give one example of using something you know to help someone (for example: I am good at maths, so I help my friend with homework).
content.teacherReflection: Did learners find the “idea” signal words themselves, and did anyone still take “I am better” as the lesson of the chapter?

classroomManagement.instructions: Read the six sentences on the board with your partner. Is it Iblis’s idea, or is it true in the story? Write each sentence in the right column.
checkQuestions: How many columns are there? (two)
What do you say in the class check? (the clue word)
classroomManagement.monitoring: Listen for the clue words “believed” and “thought” in pairs that sort correctly. A pair that puts “fire is better than clay” under “true” needs the question “Who says this?”. Note two good clue words to praise in the class check.

exitTicket: Finish: “Iblis believed ____, but useful knowledge ____ because ____.”

rubricLevels.secure: Sorts all six sentences and names a clue word such as believed.
rubricLevels.notYet: Sort two sentences together first and show the word “believed”.

rubricLevels.secure: Uses better and more valuable correctly, and couldn’t + verb.
rubricLevels.notYet: Write “good → better, valuable → more valuable” on the board as a model.

rubricLevels.secure: Uses But for a different idea and because for a reason.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give the half sentence “Iblis believed …, but …” to finish.

rubricLevels.secure: Gives one school or home example of useful knowledge.
rubricLevels.notYet: Ask “What can you do because you can read?”.

interculturalFocus.notice: Iblis says fire is better than soil, so he is better. The chapter rejects judging someone by where they come from.
interculturalFocus.compare: Ask: Have you heard someone say 'People from my town or country are better'? What does the chapter answer? Is this idea only in our culture or everywhere?
interculturalFocus.perspective: Avoid naming real groups as examples of arrogance. Keep the talk on the idea 'origin does not decide value', so no learner feels targeted.

objectives: Explain what Iblis wanted and why Allah gave Adam a wife.
Keep the two warnings apart: Be careful about Iblis / do not go near one tree.
Look at want + person + to, tell + person + to / not to, and started to + verb for something new.
Give a clear, kind warning in an everyday situation.
content.pedagogy: Use a simple “Who wants what?” map on the board: Iblis → wanted Adam to lose Allah’s love; Allah → told Adam to be careful about Iblis; Allah → told Adam and Eve not to go near one tree. Learners find each arrow in the text. Grammar is discovered with the first question, “Who did Iblis want to lose Allah’s love?”: learners see that the person after “wanted” is the one who does the action. The “not to” sentence is then learned as the shape of a clear warning.
priorKnowledge: Chapter 3: Iblis was sent far from Allah’s love and care, and Adam was now in Paradise.
anticipatedMisconceptions: There are two different warnings: One about Iblis, one about the tree.
In “He wanted Adam to lose Allah’s love, just as he had”, Adam is the one who would lose it; “just as he had” means Iblis had already lost it.
Mixing Iblis’s plan with Allah’s warning.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: want + person + to + verb (wanted Adam to lose, didn’t want Allah to be nice) · tell + person + to / not to + verb · started to + verb for something new.
Notice (Activity 1): Read “He wanted Adam to lose Allah’s love, just as he had.” Ask: “Who did Iblis want to lose Allah’s love? Who had already lost it?” Learners discover that the person after “wanted” does the action.
Build (Activities 2–3): Choose to be / to be / not to and ask “Where does not go?”, then build “Then, Adam started to feel lonely in Paradise.” and find the second “started to” sentence.
Likely errors: *wanted that Adam lose · *told Adam be careful · *told them to not go / don’t go · *started feel.
Use (Activity 4): three or four sentences with a situation, a change (started to …) and a warning (told … not to …).
content.pronunciationFocus:
Weak “to” (/tə/) inside chunks: “wanted AD-am to LOSE”, “told AD-am to be CARE-ful”.
Stress NOT in the warning: “He told Adam and Eve | NOT to go NEAR | one TREE.”
-ed endings with an extra syllable: wanted, waited, started, hated (all /ɪd/).
Word focus: LONE-ly, WON-der-ful, WARN-ing, im-AG-ine, PAR-a-dise, HAW-wa.
beforeReading: Ask: “When do parents or teachers give a warning? What words do they use?” Collect two examples (Be careful! Don’t touch …). Then predict: “In this chapter, who gives a warning, and about what?”
duringReading: Listen once: What did Iblis want?
Underline both warnings and number them 1 and 2.
Circle the two “started to” sentences.
Find why Allah gave Adam a wife (So, …).
afterReading: Quick Challenge: Choose why Allah gave Adam a wife and show the sentence before “So”.
Language Focus: Look at who Iblis wanted to lose Allah’s love (Activity 1), practise to / not to (Activity 2), build the “started to” sentence (Activity 3).
Use: Say or write a situation, a change and one clear, kind warning.
content.lessonPlan: 0–4 Hook: Two everyday warnings from learners (Be careful! Don’t …), then predict who warns whom in this chapter; 4–11 Listen once (What did Iblis want?), then read along; 11–18 “Who wants what?” map: Pairs complete four arrows on the board with quoted words (Iblis → Adam, Allah → Adam, Allah → Adam and Eve, Adam felt lonely → So …); 18–22 Quick Challenge; 22–31 Language Focus: Activity 1 as a whole-class look (Who would lose Allah’s love?), Activity 2 in pairs (where does “not” go?), Activity 3 individually, then find the second “started to” sentence; 31–37 Use: “Safety corner” in pairs, A describes a school situation (a wet floor, the science lab, the school gate), B gives a warning with “Our teacher told us (not) to …”, then they swap; 37–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: What did Iblis want, and why was he angry with Adam?
What are the two warnings in the chapter?
Why did Allah give Adam a wife?
What makes a warning clear and kind?
interactiveTips: Use the Eve (Hawwa) hotspot for why Eve is introduced and The Tree hotspot for the one warning about the tree.
Replay “He told Adam and Eve not to go near one tree.” and let learners repeat it with stress on “not”.
Keep Iblis’s plan and Allah’s warnings on different sides of the board.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Frames: “Iblis wanted Adam to ____.” “Adam started to ____.” “Allah told Adam to ____.” “Allah told Adam and Eve not to ____.”
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write four sentences with wanted … to, started to, told … to and told … not to: Two about the chapter and two about a school rule.

formativeAssessment: Names both warnings separately.
Understands who does the action after want/tell + person.
Puts “not” before “to”.
expectedResponses: Iblis wanted Adam to lose Allah’s love, just as he had.
Adam started to feel lonely in Paradise, so Allah gave him a wife.
Allah told Adam to be careful about Iblis. He told Adam and Eve not to go near one tree.
content.transferTask: Give one clear and kind warning to a younger student (for example: I told my little brother not to run near the road).
content.teacherReflection: Did learners work out who does the action after “wanted Adam to …” before I explained it, and did they keep the two warnings apart?

classroomManagement.instructions: Look at the four arrows on the board. With your partner, write the words from the story on each arrow. Who wants or tells what?
checkQuestions: Do you copy words from the story? (yes)
How many arrows? (four)
classroomManagement.monitoring: Walk around during the arrow task and check that pairs keep the two warnings apart: be careful about Iblis, and not go near one tree. In the Safety corner, listen for “told us not to”. If you hear “told us to not”, give the correct form quietly to that pair.

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “told … not to” and one with “started to”.

rubricLevels.secure: Names the warning about Iblis and the warning about the tree separately.
rubricLevels.notYet: Read the two sentences aloud and ask “Is this about Iblis or the tree?”.

rubricLevels.secure: Says who does the action after want/tell + person and puts not before to.
rubricLevels.notYet: Use two cards, “not” and “to”, and let the learner order them.

rubricLevels.secure: Finds both “started to” sentences in the chapter.
rubricLevels.notYet: Show the first one and ask the learner to find the second in the next paragraph.

rubricLevels.secure: Gives one clear, kind warning about a school place.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give the frame “Our teacher told us not to …”.

interculturalFocus.notice: Paradise is a garden with fruit and trees. Many cultures picture a perfect place as a garden: the English word paradise comes from an old Persian word for a walled garden.
interculturalFocus.compare: Ask: What is a beautiful garden like in Turkish culture (fruit trees, water, shade)? Show a picture of an English garden or a Persian garden and compare one thing.
interculturalFocus.perspective: Learners describe a garden from their own family or town. Accept village gardens, balcony pots and parks equally.

objectives: Put the events in order: lie → forgotten warning → mistake → sorry → learning → decision.
Compare Adam and Eve’s response to their mistake with Iblis’s response.
Look at If + present, … will … as Iblis’s false promise, and practise forgot, made a mistake, decided never to and the story words After a while, Unfortunately, it wasn’t on purpose.
Describe a small mistake and a better next step.
content.pedagogy: A “response ladder” organises the lesson: Learners climb from “made a mistake” to “said sorry”, “learned” and “decided never to repeat it”, each step with a quoted phrase, and put Iblis’s “opposite direction” beside it. The if-sentence is discovered as Iblis’s words: “Who says this? What must they do first? What does he promise?” The text itself answers the last question: “It was a big lie.”
priorKnowledge: Chapter 4: Allah told Adam and Eve not to go near one tree and told Adam to be careful about Iblis.
anticipatedMisconceptions: “If you eat from that one tree, you will never die” is Iblis’s lie, not a fact in the story.
“It wasn’t on purpose” does not mean the mistake did not matter: they were very sad, said sorry and learned from it.
Adam and Eve’s response and Iblis’s response go in opposite directions.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: If + present verb, … will + verb (a condition and a promised result) · forget → forgot · make a mistake (not “do”) · decided never to + verb · story words: After a while, Unfortunately, banned, it wasn’t on purpose, took an opposite direction.
Notice (Activity 1): Read Iblis’s words “If you eat from that one tree, you will never die.” Ask: “What must they do first? What does Iblis promise will happen? Is it true?” Learners say which part is the condition and which the result.
Build (Activities 2–3): Choose forgot / made / to repeat, then match the five story words with their meanings and find each one in the story.
Likely errors: *If you will eat · *forgotted · *did a mistake · *decided never repeat.
Use (Activity 4): four sentences about a simple mistake: what happened, that it wasn’t on purpose, what I learned and what I decided.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Condition and result: rise, pause, fall: “If you EAT from that one TREE↗, | you will NEV-er DIE↘.”
Contraction: “it WAS-n’t on PUR-pose” (/ˈwɒznt/).
The list about Iblis with a rise on each item: “su-PE-ri-or to↗, | SMART-er than↗ | and more im-POR-tant than the HU-man↘”.
Word focus: mis-TAKE, un-FOR-tu-nate-ly, for-GET-ful, su-PE-ri-or, OP-po-site.
beforeReading: Tell a tiny neutral story: “Ali broke a cup. It wasn’t on purpose.” Ask: “What should Ali do now?” Collect three answers (say sorry, clean it up, be careful next time) and keep them for the ladder.
duringReading: Listen once: What did Iblis tell Adam and Eve?
Mark Iblis’s promise as his words with a speech bubble in the margin.
Number the steps: mistake → very sad → said sorry → learned → decided.
Underline “However, Iblis took an opposite direction.” and find the reason (because …).
afterReading: Quick Challenge: Put four events in order, from Iblis’s lie to Adam and Eve saying sorry.
Language Focus: Look at the if-sentence (Activity 1), practise forgot / made / decided never to (Activity 2) and the story words (Activity 3).
Use: Four sentences about a simple mistake and a better next step.
content.lessonPlan: 0–4 Hook: The broken-cup story, learners suggest what Ali should do; 4–11 Listen once (What did Iblis tell them?), then read along and mark Iblis’s promise as his words; 11–19 Response ladder in pairs: Copy five steps from the text (made a mistake / very sad / said sorry / learned from their mistake / decided never to repeat it), then write Iblis’s opposite response beside it with “because he was arrogant”; 19–22 Quick Challenge; 22–31 Language Focus: Activity 1 as a whole-class look (What first? What result? Is it true?), Activities 2–3 in pairs; 31–37 Use: Pairs choose a school mistake (forgot my homework, broke a pencil case) and each learner tells the partner four ladder sentences (I made a mistake … It wasn’t on purpose … I learned … I decided never to …); 37–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: What did Iblis say, and why was it a lie?
What did Adam and Eve do after their mistake?
How was Iblis’s direction opposite?
Why is it important to say sorry and learn from a mistake?
interactiveTips: Use The Lie hotspot for Iblis’s false promise and The Mistake hotspot for Adam and Eve’s response.
Replay the if-sentence twice: Learners show one finger at the condition and two at the result.
Replay the last paragraph and ask: “Did Iblis ever say he was wrong?”

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the ladder with first words: “They made ____.” “They said ____.” “They learned ____.” “They decided never ____.” and the frame “If you ____, you will ____.”
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write five sentences comparing the two responses with However, because and decided never to, then add one true if/will sentence of your own.

formativeAssessment: Identifies the if-sentence as Iblis’s false promise.
Orders the response steps correctly.
Uses forgot, made a mistake and decided never to + verb.
expectedResponses: Iblis said, “If you eat from that one tree, you will never die.” It was a big lie.
They made a mistake, but it wasn’t on purpose. They said sorry to Allah and decided never to repeat it.
Iblis never thought he was wrong because he was arrogant.
content.transferTask: Describe a small mistake at school or at home and one responsible next step (say sorry, fix it, decide something new).
content.teacherReflection: Did learners treat the if-sentence as Iblis’s promise and not as story truth, and could they compare the two responses with evidence?

classroomManagement.instructions: With your partner, copy the five steps from the story in order. Then write what Iblis did next to each step. Use “because he was arrogant”.
checkQuestions: Where do the five steps come from? (the story)
What do you write next to them? (what Iblis did)
classroomManagement.monitoring: Check that pairs mark Iblis’s promise as his words, not as a true sentence. In the Use task, listen for “it wasn’t on purpose”. Choose one pair with a good ladder to read it to the class.

exitTicket: Complete: “I made a mistake, but it wasn’t on purpose. I learned ____, and I decided never to ____.”

rubricLevels.secure: Puts the five response steps in order.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give the first step and the last step, the learner places the other three.

rubricLevels.secure: Says the if-sentence was Iblis’s promise and a lie.
rubricLevels.notYet: Ask “Who said this? Was it true?”.

rubricLevels.secure: Uses forgot, made a mistake and decided never to + verb.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give the frame “I made a mistake. I decided never to …”.

rubricLevels.secure: Tells a small school mistake and what he or she learned.
rubricLevels.notYet: Offer two examples (forgot my homework, broke a pencil) to choose from.

interculturalFocus.notice: Adam and Eve say sorry and decide never to repeat the mistake. Saying sorry has different forms in different languages.
interculturalFocus.compare: Ask: In Turkish we say 'Özür dilerim', 'Kusura bakma', 'Pardon'. Which English phrase fits each situation (I'm sorry, Excuse me, Sorry, my mistake)? Do English speakers say sorry more often than we do?
interculturalFocus.perspective: Point out that people in some cultures apologise a lot even for small things. This is a habit of politeness, not a sign that they are weak or guilty.

objectives: List the work and responsibilities the chapter gives Adam and Eve on earth.
Separate their responsibilities from Iblis’s aim on earth.
Look at were going to + verb for future work seen from the past, one “were going to” with a list, to + verb for purpose and want + person + not to.
Name one real responsibility and its purpose.
content.pedagogy: Learners build a “job board” for life on earth: Every note is a verb from the chapter (direct, make … better, grow crops, keep animals, build, protect, help). Grammar is discovered with one question about “They were going to direct and make everything better on the planet”: “Are they walking to a place?” Learners realize that “were going to” here means future work, then notice that one “were going to” carries a whole list. Iblis’s aim goes on a note of a different color, so it never mixes with human responsibilities.
priorKnowledge: Chapter 5: Adam and Eve said sorry and wanted Allah to excuse them.
anticipatedMisconceptions: “Were going to” here does not mean going to a place.
Iblis’s aim (people not remembering Allah) is not a human responsibility.
Adding jobs that are not in the chapter.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: were going to + verb = future work seen from the past · one “were going to” + a list (build …, protect … and help …) · to + verb for purpose (to live there, to rule on earth) · want + person + not to + verb.
Notice (Activity 1): Read “They were going to direct and make everything better on the planet.” Ask: “Are they walking to a place? When is this work — before or after they came to earth?”
Build (Activities 2–3): Build “They were going to build houses, protect nature and help the weak.” (count the jobs, find the commas and “and”), then choose to / to / not to and ask “Which one answers Why?”
Likely errors: *for live there, *for to live · *wanted people don’t remember · *protect the nature.
Use (Activity 4): four sentences about useful responsibilities: A plan (I am going to …), a purpose (to …) and a job for other people.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Chunk the list, rising on each job and falling on the last: “They were going to BUILD HOUS-es↗, | pro-TECT NA-ture↗ | and HELP the WEAK↘.”
Weak forms: “were” (/wə/) and “to” (/tə/): “they were going to di-RECT”.
-ing: /ɪŋ/ without an extra /g/ sound: using, going.
Word focus: PLAN-et, NA-ture, HOUS-es, RUL-ers, DAI-ly, pro-TECT.
beforeReading: Ask: “If you start life in a new place, what work is waiting for you?” Pairs name two jobs. After reading, they tick any job the chapter also names.
duringReading: Listen once: Where did Allah put Adam and Eve, and why?
Underline every job verb (direct, make … better, grow, keep, build, protect, help).
Box the purpose phrases “to live there” and “to rule on earth”.
Mark Iblis’s aim in a different color.
afterReading: Quick Challenge: Decide true or false: On earth, Iblis followed Adam and Eve and was still around them.
Language Focus: Look at “were going to” (Activity 1), build the list sentence (Activity 2), practise to / not to (Activity 3).
Use: Four sentences about useful responsibilities at school or at home.
content.lessonPlan: 0–4 Hook: Pairs name two jobs for a new life in a new place; 4–11 Listen once (Where did Allah put them? Why?), then read along; 11–18 Job board: Pairs write each job from the chapter on a note or in a grid, then Iblis’s aim on a note of another color, whole-class check against the text; 18–22 Quick Challenge; 22–31 Language Focus: Activity 1 as a whole-class look (walking to a place or future work?), Activity 2 in pairs (count the jobs), Activity 3 individually (which one answers Why?); 31–37 Use: “Class jobs” in groups of four, each learner says one real responsibility with a purpose (I water the plants to keep them alive), the group chooses the most useful one and reports it; 37–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why did Allah put Adam and Eve on earth?
Which jobs are about nature and which are about people?
What did Iblis want on earth?
Which of these jobs can we still do today?
interactiveTips: Use the Earth hotspot for life on the planet and the Work hotspot for the list of jobs.
Replay the list sentence and ask learners to count the jobs on their fingers.
Point to the second paragraph when learners mix Iblis’s aim with human responsibilities.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Verb cards (grow, keep, build, protect, help) and the frames “They were going to ____.” “They were using land to ____.” “Iblis wanted people not to ____.”
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write four sentences: Two about the chapter with were going to + a list, and two about your own responsibilities with to + verb for purpose.

formativeAssessment: Lists responsibilities from the text only.
Explains that “were going to” is future work here, not movement.
Uses to + verb (not for + verb) for purpose.
expectedResponses: Allah put them on earth to live there.
They were going to build houses, protect nature and help the weak.
They were using land to grow crops and keep animals.
Iblis wanted people not to remember Allah in their daily lives.
content.transferTask: Name one responsibility at school or at home and its purpose (for example: I clean the board to help my teacher).
content.teacherReflection: Did learners discover that “were going to” means future work here, and did the values come from real verbs in the chapter?

classroomManagement.instructions: Write each job from the story on a note. Write Iblis’s aim on a note of a different color. Then check with the text.
checkQuestions: What goes on the different color note? (Iblis’s aim)
Do you add jobs that are not in the story? (no)
classroomManagement.monitoring: Check that the job notes come from the text: build buildings, protect nature, help the weak, grow crops, keep animals. In groups of four, listen for “to + verb” after the job. If you hear “for water the plants”, repeat the sentence correctly for the group.

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “to + verb” for purpose and one with “wanted … not to”.

rubricLevels.secure: Lists the jobs from the text only.
rubricLevels.notYet: Read the paragraph aloud and let the learner raise a hand at each job.

rubricLevels.secure: Says “were going to” is future work here, not walking to a place.
rubricLevels.notYet: Ask “Are they walking, or is it a plan for work?”.

rubricLevels.secure: Uses to + verb for purpose.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give the frame “I water the plants to …”.

rubricLevels.secure: Gives one real responsibility with a reason.
rubricLevels.notYet: Ask “What is your job at home?” and help with to + verb.

interculturalFocus.notice: On earth Adam and Eve farm, look after animals and care for people. Farming and care for nature are part of every culture.
interculturalFocus.compare: Ask: What do people grow or raise near your town (wheat in Konya, hazelnuts on the Black Sea)? What do farmers grow in another country you know?
interculturalFocus.perspective: Learners who live in cities may know little about farming. Let them choose another job that cares for nature, such as a park worker.

objectives: Say what Adam taught people and what Adam and Eve taught their children.
Explain why they warned their children against Iblis.
Look at teach + person + to, warn + person + against, “X, not Y”, and the time phrases for many years / Then / After the death of … to follow the story.
Give simple, kind guidance with a reason.
content.pedagogy: Draw a three-part timeline: Life on earth (for many years) → Adam the first Messenger (Then) → later messengers (After the death of Adam). Learners place quoted sentences on it. The language grows from the teaching: Learners collect what was taught and notice the small words after teach and warn (to / against) before you name the pattern. “Their enemy, not their friend” shows how a short phrase says what is true and what is not.
priorKnowledge: Chapter 6: Adam and Eve lived on earth, and Iblis was still around.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Do not add names or stories of later messengers: The chapter only says that Allah sent many other messengers and all the prophets took the same way.
“Warned their children against Iblis” means “told them to stay away from him”, not “fought against him”.
“Hard days” means difficult days.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: teach + person + to + verb (teaching people to be honest, taught their children to behave well) · warn + person + against + danger · X, not Y (their enemy, not their friend) · time phrases for many years, Then, After the death of ….
Notice (Activity 1): Read “They also warned their children against Iblis because Iblis was their enemy, not their friend.” Ask: “What did they tell the children to stay away from? Is Iblis a friend?” Learners then find the small words after teach and warn (to / against).
Build (Activities 2–3): Match the time and life phrases with their meanings, then order five sentences from Adam to the later messengers with the help of Then and After.
Likely errors: *teaching people for be honest, *taught that behave · *warned them from Iblis · *their enemy, no their friend · *After Adam die.
Use (Activity 4): four sentences that teach, warn and give a reason in daily life.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Chunk the teaching list, rising on each item: “to be HON-est↗, | do GOOD↗, | stop BAD↗ | and AL-ways re-MEM-ber al-LAH↘”.
Contrastive stress: “their EN-e-my, | NOT their FRIEND”.
Silent h in honest (/ˈɒnɪst/).
Word focus: MES-sen-ger, HON-est, be-HAVE, EN-e-my, PROPH-ets, DIF-fi-cult.
beforeReading: Ask: “What does a good teacher do?” Collect verbs on the board (teaches, helps, warns, explains). Then: “In this chapter, who teaches, and what do they teach?”
duringReading: Listen once: Who did Allah make His first Messenger?
List only what the chapter says Adam taught people and what Adam and Eve taught their children.
Underline the warning and the reason (because …).
Circle the time phrases: for many years, Then, After the death of ….
afterReading: Quick Challenge: Choose why Adam and Eve warned their children against Iblis.
Language Focus: Look at teach … to / warn … against / not (Activity 1), match the time phrases (Activity 2), order the story from Adam to the later messengers (Activity 3).
Use: Four sentences of kind guidance with a reason.
content.lessonPlan: 0–4 Hook: “What does a good teacher do?” verbs on the board; 4–11 Listen once (Who became the first Messenger?), then read along; 11–18 Timeline in pairs: Three boxes (for many years / Then / After the death of Adam), each with one quoted sentence, then the teachings listed under Adam’s box; 18–22 Quick Challenge; 22–31 Language Focus: Activity 1 as a whole-class look (What small word comes after teach? after warn?), Activities 2–3 in pairs, reading the ordered sentences aloud; 31–37 Use: “Advice for a new student” in pairs, each pair writes four sentences (Our teachers teach us to … / They warn us against … because … / Be kind, not rude.) and one pair reads to the class; 37–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: What did Adam teach people?
What did Adam and Eve teach their children, and why did they warn them against Iblis?
What did all the prophets want?
Who teaches and warns us in our lives, and why?
interactiveTips: Use the Messenger hotspot for “Allah made Adam His first Messenger” and the Teaching hotspot for what was taught.
Replay the teaching list and ask learners to count the four things on their fingers.
Stop after “not their friend” and let learners say it with stress on “not”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Frames: “Adam taught people to ____.” “They warned their children against ____ because ____.” “Iblis was their ____, not their ____.”
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write four guidance sentences for a younger student with teach … to, warn … against, because and “X, not Y”.

formativeAssessment: Lists only the teachings in the text.
Uses teach … to and warn … against correctly.
Follows the story order with Then and After.
expectedResponses: He started teaching people to be honest, do good, stop bad and always remember Allah.
They taught their children to behave well for the love of Allah and to thank Him.
They warned their children against Iblis because Iblis was their enemy, not their friend.
After the death of Adam (pbuh), Allah sent many other messengers.
content.transferTask: Give kind guidance to a younger learner and explain why (for example: I warn my brother against playing near the road because it is dangerous).
content.teacherReflection: Did learners notice the small words after teach and warn themselves, and did they keep to what the chapter says about the later messengers?

classroomManagement.instructions: Draw three boxes with your partner: for many years, Then, After the death of Adam. Copy one sentence from the story into each box.
checkQuestions: How many boxes? (three)
Where do you write Adam’s teachings? (under his box)
classroomManagement.monitoring: Check that the teachings under Adam’s box are from the text: be honest, do good, stop bad, remember Allah. In the Use task, listen for “warn us against”. Collect two good sentences on the board for the class.

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “warn … against … because …” and one with “X, not Y”.

rubricLevels.secure: Lists only the teachings in the text.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give the four teachings on cards mixed with one that is not in the text.

rubricLevels.secure: Uses teach … to and warn … against correctly.
rubricLevels.notYet: Show the two patterns on the board as gap sentences.

rubricLevels.secure: Follows the story order with Then and After.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give the three box titles in order and let the learner match one sentence to each.

rubricLevels.secure: Gives one piece of school advice with a reason.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give the frame “They warn us against … because …”.

interculturalFocus.notice: Adam teaches his children and warns them. Parents passing on values is part of every family culture.
interculturalFocus.compare: Ask: Which sayings do older people in your family repeat (atasözleri)? Do you know an English saying with the same idea, for example 'Better safe than sorry'?
interculturalFocus.perspective: Families teach in different ways. Learners share only a saying they are happy to share, not private family matters.

content.chapter: Chapter 8 — Story of Habil and Qabil
objectives: Describe the two brothers: What each was like, his job and his offering.
Explain the chapter’s lesson: “Real goodness is giving the best and the most loved.”
Look at was + adjective (what someone is like) and was / became + a + job, then practise loved + -ing, had to, the best and healthiest, and but for contrast.
Describe a good choice in your own life.
content.pedagogy: Use a three-row grid (What was he like? / His job / His offering) with one column for each brother, filled only with words from the text. Learners then discover in Activity 1 that “was kind” and “was a farmer” look alike but do different jobs: an adjective describes a person, “a + job” names work. Keep the jobs neutral: Being a shepherd or a farmer is not good or bad; the difference is in what each brother chose to give.
priorKnowledge: Chapter 7: Adam and Eve had lots of children and taught them to behave well.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Farming is not bad work: The chapter criticises Qabil’s small offering, not his job.
Adding details about the brothers that are not in the chapter.
“They had to offer an offering” means it was necessary to solve the problem.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: was + adjective (kind, gentle, jealous) vs was / became + a + job · became = a change (When they grew up, …) · love + -ing · had to + verb (past necessity) · good → the best, healthy → the healthiest · but for two different ideas.
Notice (Activity 1): learners sort four sentences into “What was he like?” / “What was his job?” Ask: “What is the difference between ‘Habil was kind’ and ‘Qabil was a farmer’? Why does the chapter say ‘became’?”
Build (Activities 2–3): Choose taking / had to / best and healthiest, then complete “… as a gift for Allah, but Qabil brought just a handful of his crops.”
Likely errors: *Habil was a kind · *Qabil was farmer · *loved take care · *must to offer · *goodest, *most healthy.
Use (Activity 4): four sentences describing a person, a responsibility (had to …) and a good choice (the best …).
content.pronunciationFocus:
Contrastive stress on the two gifts: “Habil brought his BEST and HEALTH-i-est SHEEP | but Qabil brought just a HAND-ful of his CROPS.”
The lesson sentence slowly: “REAL GOOD-ness is GIV-ing the BEST | and the MOST LOVED.”
In shepherd the h is silent (/ˈʃepəd/).
Word focus: SHEP-herd, FARM-er, OF-fer-ing, JEAL-ous, HEALTH-i-est, dis-a-GREE-ment.
beforeReading: Write two gifts on the board: “my best pen” / “an old broken pencil”. Ask: “Which gift shows that you care? Why?” Keep the answer for the end of the chapter.
duringReading: Listen once: What was each brother’s job?
Fill the three-row grid for Habil and Qabil with words from the text.
Underline “To solve the problem, they had to offer an offering to Allah.”
Box the lesson sentence at the end.
afterReading: Quick Challenge: Match each brother with his work and his offering.
Language Focus: Look at what he was like vs his job (Activity 1), practise loved taking / had to / the best and healthiest (Activity 2) and the but-sentence (Activity 3).
Use: Four sentences about a person, a responsibility and a good choice in your life.
content.lessonPlan: 0–4 Hook: Two gifts on the board (my best pen / an old broken pencil), learners vote and say why; 4–11 Listen once (What was each brother’s job?), then read along; 11–18 Brothers grid in pairs: Three rows (What was he like? / His job / His offering), two columns, only words from the text, then learners read one row aloud with “but”; 18–22 Quick Challenge; 22–31 Language Focus: Activity 1 as a whole-class look (kind or a farmer — what is the difference?), Activities 2–3 in pairs; 31–37 Use: “Giving my best” think-pair-share, each learner thinks of a time they had to do something and gave their best (a present, a project, help at home), writes three sentences and tells a partner; 37–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: How were the two brothers different?
What did each brother bring, and what does “just a handful” tell us?
What does “Real goodness is giving the best and the most loved” mean for you?
Is a farmer’s job worse than a shepherd’s job? What made the difference?
interactiveTips: Use the Habil hotspot and the Qabil hotspot to check the grid, one brother at a time.
Replay the offering sentence and ask learners to raise a hand at “but”.
Read the lesson sentence together once, slowly.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Frames: “Habil was ____. He became a ____. He brought ____.” “Qabil was ____. He was a ____. He brought ____.”
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write five sentences comparing the brothers with was + adjective, became + a + job, had to, the best and but.

formativeAssessment: Separates description, job and offering.
Uses “a” with jobs and no “a” with adjectives alone.
Uses had to and the best / the healthiest correctly.
expectedResponses: Habil was kind, gentle and loved taking care of animals. He became a shepherd.
Qabil was mostly jealous. He was a farmer.
Habil brought his best and healthiest sheep, but Qabil brought just a handful of his crops.
Real goodness is giving the best and the most loved.
content.transferTask: Describe one situation where you give your best, and label it clearly as your own example.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners discover the difference between “was kind” and “was a farmer”, and did they avoid judging the brothers’ jobs?

classroomManagement.instructions: With your partner, complete the brothers grid. Use only words from the story. Then read one row aloud with “but”.
checkQuestions: How many rows? (three)
Can you use your own words in the grid? (no, only story words)
classroomManagement.monitoring: Check that “kind” and “a shepherd” are in different rows. Listen for “He was a farmer” and “He was jealous” in the read-aloud. In think-pair-share, listen for “had to” and “the best”, and note one good example.

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “had to” and one with “the best”.

rubricLevels.secure: Fills the grid with words from the text only.
rubricLevels.notYet: Fill the first row together, the learner finishes the others.

rubricLevels.secure: Uses a with jobs and no a with adjectives alone.
rubricLevels.notYet: Ask “Is shepherd a job or a feeling?”.

rubricLevels.secure: Uses had to and the best or the healthiest correctly.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give the frame “I had to … and I gave my best.”.

rubricLevels.secure: Tells about one time he or she gave the best.
rubricLevels.notYet: Offer three choices: a present, a project, help at home.

interculturalFocus.notice: The brothers have two jobs: farmer and shepherd. In English Bible tradition the brothers are called Cain and Abel; in Turkish they are Kabil and Habil.
interculturalFocus.compare: Ask: Why does the same person have different names in different languages? Can you think of another example (İstanbul / Constantinople, Mısır / Egypt)?
interculturalFocus.perspective: A shepherd and a farmer were both respected jobs. Do not let learners rank jobs; the chapter judges the gift, not the job.

objectives: Follow the events calmly: Qabil’s anger → Habil’s refusal to harm → Habil’s death → Qabil’s sadness and panic → the crow.
Explain Habil’s choice and his reasons (“You are my brother, and I fear Allah.”).
Look at won’t for a clear refusal, the feeling phrases (not angry anymore, started to panic, worse than), became + adjective, the past forms became / sent, and “I don’t know what I should do”.
Practise safe language for anger, calming down and asking for help.
content.pedagogy: Set a calm frame before listening: We focus on choices, feelings and the lesson, not on the violent moment. Play or read the chapter once without stopping; no line is acted out, drawn or repeated for practice. A “feelings line” (very angry → not angry anymore → so sad → panic → cried) carries the meaning work. Grammar starts from Habil’s words: “Past or future? Is he not able to fight, or does he choose not to?” so learners discover that won’t shows a clear choice.
priorKnowledge: Chapter 8: the brothers’ disagreement and their two offerings.
anticipatedMisconceptions: “I won’t fight back” is a choice, not weakness: Habil was not “unable” to fight.
“Not angry anymore” means the anger stopped. It does not mean that Qabil was happy.
“I am worse than this crow” means that even the bird knew what to do.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: won’t + verb = a clear “no” about the future · feeling phrases (not angry anymore, started to panic, worse than) · became + adjective (became very angry) · special past forms became, sent · I don’t know what I should do (asking for the right action).
Notice (Activity 1): Read Habil’s words “I won’t fight back or harm you.” Ask: “Past or future? Is Habil not able, or does he choose not to? What are his reasons?”
Build (Activities 2–3): Match the feeling phrases with their meanings and place them on the feelings line, then complete became / should / sent and say why “becomed” and “sended” are wrong.
Likely errors: *I won’t to fight · *becomed, *sended · *I don’t know what should I do · *worse from this crow.
Use (Activity 4): four sentences about a safe everyday situation: A choice (I won’t …), a feeling (I became …), a question (What should I do?) and help (My teacher showed me …).
content.pronunciationFocus:
Hear the difference: “will” (/wɪl/) and “won’t” (/wəʊnt/, long vowel + t): “I WON’T fight BACK | or HARM you.”
The reasons with a pause: “You are my BROTH-er, | and I FEAR al-LAH.”
The question chunk: “I don’t KNOW | what I should DO”.
Word focus: AN-ger, PAN-ic, DIG-ging, BROTH-er (/ʌ/, /ð/), crow (/krəʊ/, like “grow”), worse (/wɜːs/).
Read the whole chapter in a calm, even voice.
beforeReading: Set the calm frame: “Today’s chapter is sad. We will listen once, calmly. Then we talk about choices and feelings.” Ask: “What can we do when we feel very angry?” Collect safe ideas (stop, breathe, walk away, talk to an adult).
duringReading: Listen once without stopping: Which brother chose not to fight?
Mark Habil’s answer and his two reasons.
Build the feelings line for Qabil: Very angry → not angry anymore → so sad → panic → cried.
Find what the crow showed Qabil.
afterReading: Quick Challenge: Choose why Habil said he would not fight back.
Language Focus: Look at won’t (Activity 1), match the feeling phrases (Activity 2), practise became / should / sent (Activity 3).
Use: Four sentences about a safe everyday situation with a choice, a feeling, a question and help.
content.lessonPlan: 0–4 Calm frame: The teacher says the chapter is sad, learners share safe ways to calm down when angry; 4–11 Listen once without stopping (Which brother chose not to fight?), then read along quietly; 11–18 Feelings line in pairs: Five cards for Qabil (very angry / not angry anymore / felt so sad / started to panic / cried) put in order, plus one card for Habil’s choice with his two reasons; 18–22 Quick Challenge; 22–31 Language Focus: Activity 1 as a whole-class look (past or future? not able or does not want?), Activities 2–3 in pairs; 31–37 Use: “Stop and ask” in pairs, learners choose a safe everyday problem (a lost bag, an argument in a game) and write four sentences (I won’t … / I became … / I don’t know what I should do. / My teacher showed me …); 37–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: What did Habil say, and what were his reasons?
How did Qabil’s feelings change when he was not angry anymore?
What did the crow show Qabil?
What can we do when we feel very angry?
interactiveTips: Use The Crow hotspot for what the crow did and the Panic hotspot for Qabil’s changing feelings.
Replay Habil’s answer, not Qabil’s threat; do not ask learners to repeat the threat or the violent sentences.
Do not act out, draw or add details to the violent part of the chapter.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Feelings cards with simple face drawings and the frames “Habil said, ‘I won’t ____.’” “Qabil became ____.” “Then he started to ____.”
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write five safe sentences about calming down with won’t, became + adjective, started to, should and one sentence with “worse than” or “better than”.

formativeAssessment: Tells the events in order calmly, without violent detail.
Explains won’t as Habil’s choice and gives his reasons.
Uses became / sent and the word order “what I should do”.
expectedResponses: Habil said, “I won’t fight back or harm you. You are my brother, and I fear Allah.”
Soon, Qabil was not angry anymore, and he felt so sad. But he also started to panic.
Allah sent a crow. The crow showed Qabil the way to put his brother’s body in the hole.
content.transferTask: Give a safe example of stopping when you are angry and asking someone what you should do.
content.teacherReflection: Was the sad content handled calmly, and did learners understand won’t as a brave choice rather than weakness?

classroomManagement.instructions: With your partner, put the five feeling cards for Qabil in order. Then add one card for Habil’s choice and write his two reasons.
checkQuestions: How many cards for Qabil? (five)
Do we act out the story? (no)
classroomManagement.monitoring: Keep the room calm. Listen for the order “very angry, not angry anymore, felt so sad, started to panic, cried”. If a pair repeats violent detail, bring them back to the feelings cards. In the Use task, check that learners choose a safe everyday problem.

exitTicket: Write one “I won’t …” sentence about a good choice and one “I don’t know what I should do” sentence with a helpful answer.

rubricLevels.secure: Orders the feeling cards and tells the events calmly.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give the first and last cards.

rubricLevels.secure: Explains that won’t is Habil’s choice and gives his two reasons.
rubricLevels.notYet: Read Habil’s sentence aloud and ask “Can he fight? Does he want to?”.

rubricLevels.secure: Uses became and feeling phrases such as not angry anymore.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give the frame “He became … and then …”.

rubricLevels.secure: Says one safe way to ask for help.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give the frame “I don’t know what I should do. I ask …”.

interculturalFocus.notice: The crow shows Qabil how to bury his brother. Burying the dead with care is shared by many cultures.
interculturalFocus.compare: Ask only a gentle, general question: Which animals appear in stories in Turkish culture as teachers or messengers (the crow, the hoopoe, the wolf)? Is there a similar animal in an English story?
interculturalFocus.perspective: This is a sad chapter. Do not ask about funerals or personal loss. Keep the comparison to animals in stories.

objectives: Say what happened to Adam’s family and how Adam continued his life.
Find the chapter’s explicit lessons (stay away from jealousy, control anger, be well-behaved and kind) and link each one to an earlier event.
Look at special past forms (went, became, lost, took), should for advice, had to, still, tell + person + to and help us to.
Give two pieces of advice and label them as your own.
content.pedagogy: The last chapter is a synthesis. After a calm first listening, learners build “lesson ← event” pairs: Each explicit lesson (stay away from jealousy, not get angry quickly, be kind to others) is matched with an earlier event (Qabil was mostly jealous, Qabil became very angry, Habil brought his best). Grammar is discovered through function: Learners decide “Is this advice, something necessary, or something that continues?” for should / had to / still before the forms are named.
priorKnowledge: Chapters 8–9: the two brothers, the offerings and what happened after Qabil’s anger.
anticipatedMisconceptions: “He went far away” is about Qabil, not Adam.
“He lost both of his sons on the same day” means Habil died and Qabil went away.
“Still” means the message continues until now; it did not stop.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: special past forms (go → went, become → became, lose → lost, take → took) · should + verb for advice (no “to”) · had to + verb for past necessity · still = continues until now · tell + person + to + verb · help us to + verb.
Notice (Activity 1): learners match the four verbs with their past forms. Ask: “Which past forms are very different from the verb?” (go → went, take → took), then read “His children and grandchildren took his message all over the world.” and ask: “Now or in the past? How do we know?”
Build (Activities 2–3): Choose should / had to / still, asking for each one “advice, necessary or continues?”, then build “It tells them to be well-behaved and kind to others.” and find a second “to” pattern (help us to live).
Likely errors: *should to stay · *must to continue · *taked, *losed · *it tells them be.
Use (Activity 4): four sentences: One piece of advice (should), one past duty (had to), one change (got old / became) and how something helps you (helps me to …).
content.pronunciationFocus:
Past forms with clear endings: went /t/, lost /st/; took has a short sound /tʊk/.
“Should” is weak (/ʃəd/) and the l is silent: “good PEO-ple should STAY a-WAY from JEAL-ous-y”.
Chunk: “This MES-sage | STILL ad-VIS-es PEO-ple | to LOVE and re-SPECT al-LAH.”
Word focus: JEAL-ous-y, well-be-HAVED, MES-sage, ad-VIS-es, HON-est.
beforeReading: Ask: “Which lessons from Habil and Qabil do you remember?” Pairs write one lesson on a card. After reading, they check whether the chapter says the same.
duringReading: Listen once: Who is “He” in the first sentence? (Qabil)
Underline the advice sentence with “should”.
Mark what Adam had to do and what happened over the years.
Box the two sentences about the message today (still …, It tells them to …).
afterReading: Quick Challenge: Decide true or false: Adam’s message stayed only with his own family.
Language Focus: Look at the past forms (Activity 1), practise should / had to / still (Activity 2), build the “tells them to” sentence (Activity 3).
Use: Four sentences with advice, a past duty, a change and how stories help you.

Then follow the whole-book sequence: Knowledge Check → Vocabulary Challenge → Language Review → Master Glossary (Parts 1–2) → Final Challenge. The first three are practice; the Final Challenge is the summative task.
content.lessonPlan: 0–4 Recall: Pairs write one lesson from Habil and Qabil on a card; 4–11 Listen once (Who is “He” in the first sentence? What happened to Adam?), then read along; 11–18 Lesson ← event matching in pairs: Three lessons from the chapter (stay away from jealousy / not get angry quickly / be well-behaved and kind to others) each linked to one event from Chapters 8–9 with the chapter number; 18–22 Quick Challenge; 22–31 Language Focus: Activity 1 individually, Activity 2 as a whole-class look (advice, necessary or continues?), Activity 3 in pairs plus finding “help us to live”; 31–37 Use: “Advice wall”, each learner writes one piece of advice for the class with should and one sentence “Stories help me to …” on a sticky note, then a quick gallery walk; 37–40 Exit ticket and a short look at the order of the review pages.
discussionPoints: Why was Adam very sad?
What does the story tell good people to do?
How does Adam’s message continue today?
Which earlier event shows why we should control our anger?
interactiveTips: Use the Adam’s Family hotspot for what happened to the family and The Message hotspot for how the message continues.
Replay the first three sentences and ask who each “He” is.
Keep the real review order and do not skip the two Master Glossary pages before the Final Challenge.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Frames: “Good people should ____.” “Adam had to ____.” “The message still ____.” “Stories help us to ____.”
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write five sentences that link two lessons to earlier events (In Chapter 8 / 9, …) using should, had to and still.

formativeAssessment: Links each lesson to an earlier event.
Uses should without “to” and had to for the past.
Uses still for something that continues.
expectedResponses: He lost both of his sons on the same day.
The story tells us that good people should stay away from jealousy and not get angry quickly.
He had to continue his life. He got old over the years.
His children and grandchildren took his message all over the world. This message still advises people to love and respect Allah.
content.transferTask: Write two age-appropriate pieces of advice with should and label them as your own application.
content.teacherReflection: Did the lesson connect the explicit lessons with earlier events, and did learners work out what should / had to / still do before I named them?

classroomManagement.instructions: With your partner, match each lesson to one event from Chapter 8 or 9. Write the chapter number next to it.
checkQuestions: What do you write next to the event? (the chapter number)
How many lessons? (three)
classroomManagement.monitoring: Check that each lesson links to a real earlier event, for example jealousy to Qabil’s offering. On the advice wall, check for “should” with no “to”. Read three notes aloud during the gallery walk.

exitTicket: Write one lesson from the story with “should” and one earlier event that supports it.

rubricLevels.secure: Links each lesson to an event and names the chapter.
rubricLevels.notYet: Show the events from Chapters 8 and 9 on cards to choose from.

rubricLevels.secure: Uses should without to, had to for the past and still for something that continues.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give three gap sentences, one for each word.

rubricLevels.secure: Uses went, became, lost and took correctly.
rubricLevels.notYet: Let the learner match base and past forms on cards first.

rubricLevels.secure: Writes one piece of advice and marks it as his or her own.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give the frame “I think we should …”.

interculturalFocus.notice: Adam's message spreads to his children and continues. Every culture keeps stories that are told again and again.
interculturalFocus.compare: Ask: Which stories did your grandparents tell you? Is there an English story that people tell children again and again (a fairy tale, a fable)?
interculturalFocus.perspective: Show that stories travel between cultures: the same fable can be in Turkish, English and Arabic. Learners name one story they think children everywhere could enjoy.

metadata.title: Teacher Guide — Prophet Adam (A2)
metadata.subtitle: TYMM-aligned A2 guide with chapter-specific support, inductive grammar (Look → Practise → Use) and 40-minute lesson plans
metadata.estimatedDuration: 10 chapter units, each planned for one 40-minute lesson. The whole-book review pages (Knowledge Check, Vocabulary Challenge, Language Review, Master Glossary, Final Challenge) follow separately.
metadata.targetAudience: Lower-secondary learners studying English at approximately CEFR A2.
metadata.targetLearners: Learners who can follow a short, supported story, find information in it and produce short spoken or written sentences with frames and oral rehearsal.
metadata.purpose: Develop A2 listening, reading, speaking and writing through the story of Adam (pbuh): meaning and evidence first, then the chapter’s own Language Focus, then short, real-life use of the language and a value connected to a concrete action — without adding facts outside the story.
metadata.approachDesc: Every chapter follows the TYMM route. YDAB1 listening and YDAB2 reading build meaning and evidence first; the Quick Challenge checks understanding. Grammar is then learned inductively, as the Maarif Model expects for English: in the Language Focus, learners first LOOK at a form in a real chapter sentence and answer one meaning question (Did it happen, or was it a plan? Who does the action? Is it advice or something necessary?), say the rule in their own simple words and only then hear it confirmed; next they PRACTISE it in short, controlled tasks with story sentences; finally they USE it in four short sentences of YDAB3 speaking and YDAB4 writing about their own life. At A2 every step is short and concrete, with minimal grammar terms, strong sentence frames and oral rehearsal in pairs before writing. See https://tymm.meb.gov.tr/beceriler/yabanci-dil-alan-becerileri.
metadata.assessmentEvidence: 10 Quick Challenges, evidence tasks (event strips, grids, timelines, feelings line), Language Focus answers and the four-sentence Use task, exit tickets, Knowledge Check, Vocabulary Challenge, Language Review and the Final Challenge.

formative: Evidence tasks: event order, sorting, grids and timelines

readingFramework.before: Activate only what the chapter needs with one short, chapter-specific hook: An object, a question from daily life, a quick recall of the last chapter or a prediction.
readingFramework.during: Listen once for gist with one simple question, then read along and do one evidence task that fits the chapter (order event strips, sort sentences, fill a grid, build a timeline or a feelings line). Do not stop to teach every word.
readingFramework.after: Complete the Quick Challenge, then the chapter’s Language Focus (Look → Practise → Use), then a short spoken or written transfer about the learners’ own life, and finish with an exit ticket.

vocabularyApproach.selection: Prioritise the chapter Word Notes and only the extra words learners need for the evidence task.
vocabularyApproach.method: Let learners guess meaning from the sentence, the image, a hotspot or a mime before giving a definition, then check with the Word Note.
vocabularyApproach.recycling: Reuse the words in the Use task, exit tickets, the Vocabulary Challenge and the Master Glossary.

metadata.grammarApproach: Inductive and text-based, with very few grammar terms at A2. Start from the story sentence, ask one meaning question, let learners say the rule in simple words (a quick word in Turkish is fine), then confirm it and practise it in context. The app shows the rule explanation only after learners answer. Do not replace the chapter work with unrelated grammar drills.
grammarSequence: Ch1: past forms (said, began, got, created); finished event vs plan (collected, shaped / was going to create); because, After that, Because of this
Ch2: could (was able to); wiser than, learned more than; taught + person + to; thought + sentence for an opinion; But … didn’t think so
Ch3: idea signals (thought, believed, continued saying) vs chapter truth; better, more valuable; couldn’t + verb; But and because
Ch4: want + person + to; tell + person + to / not to; started to + verb
Ch5: If + present, … will … (Iblis’s promise); forgot, made a mistake, decided never to; After a while, Unfortunately, on purpose, took an opposite direction
Ch6: were going to (future work seen from the past); one “were going to” + a list; to + verb for purpose; want + person + not to
Ch7: teach + person + to; warn + person + against; X, not Y; time phrases (for many years, Then, After the death of …)
Ch8: was + adjective vs was / became + a + job; love + -ing; had to; the best and healthiest; but for contrast
Ch9: won’t for a clear choice; feeling phrases (not angry anymore, started to panic, worse than); became + adjective; became, sent; I don’t know what I should do
Ch10: went, became, lost, took; should (advice); had to; still; tell + person + to; help us to

skillsFocus.reading: TYMM YDAB2: find explicit information, follow the order of events, compare two people or two views and connect a reason with a result.
skillsFocus.listening: TYMM YDAB1: follow the narration for gist, key details, order and the chapter’s target sentences.
skillsFocus.speaking: TYMM YDAB3: say three or four clear A2 sentences after pair rehearsal: retell, compare, give a reason, warn or advise.
skillsFocus.writing: TYMM YDAB4: write short connected sentences with the chapter’s patterns about the learners’ own life, then check them with a partner.

valuesFocus: D14 Respect — respectful treatment of people and difference
D16 Responsibility — responsibility for work, people and nature
D6 Honesty — truthfulness, useful knowledge and an honest response to mistakes
D10 Humility — rejecting arrogance and admitting mistakes
D5 Sensitivity — care for nature, for the weak and for other people’s feelings
D20 Helpfulness — helping the weak and giving one’s best
