D12 Patience — controlling anger and reacting calmly
D9 Compassion — not harming others and asking for help
languageFocus: Each of the 10 story chapters has an active Language Focus set built as Look → Practise → Use: Three short activities with story sentences and a final Say It task.
Do the Language Focus after listening, reading and the Quick Challenge, never before the meaning is clear.
Always start from the story sentence and ask what the form does before naming it.
Let learners answer first; the explanation after each answer confirms the rule they have found.
At A2 the Use step is four short sentences about the learners’ own life, rehearsed orally in pairs before anyone writes.
metadata.differentiationNotes: Reduce the language load without lowering the thinking goal: One evidence sentence at a time, audio replay, word cards, sentence frames and oral rehearsal before writing. Extend by adding one more pattern or one more reason, never by adding facts from outside the book.

sensitiveNotes.title: Source fidelity and respectful teaching
notes: Keep all religious and historical content within the story text; do not add legends, names or details from other versions of the story.
Qur’anic content, the words of Allah reported in the story, prophetic sayings and prayers are read, explained and matched to meanings; they are never gapped, corrected or rewritten.
Do not depict the Prophets (pbuh) or ask learners to draw or act them; use event strips, grids and timelines instead.
Treat Iblis’s words (“I am better than Adam”, “If you eat from that one tree, you will never die”) as his claims and lies, never as story truth.
Handle Chapter 9 calmly: Read it once, do not act out, draw or repeat the violent lines, and focus on choices, feelings and asking for help.
Learners’ own examples and value transfer are their applications, not new religious facts.

globalCitizenship.title: Global Citizenship and Cultural Bridges
globalCitizenship.description: The story of Adam (pbuh) begins with one human family. It gives learners simple, story-based ways to talk about living together: Respecting difference, using knowledge for good, caring for the earth and solving problems without harm.

themes.title: One family, many colors:
themes.description: Chapter 1 says humans have different skin colors because the soil came from different parts of the earth. Practise describing difference with respect and without saying one group is better.

themes.title: Knowledge for good:
themes.description: Chapter 3 says useful knowledge makes people great because with it humans can do good and stop bad. Talk about knowledge that helps people in your school and town.

themes.title: Caring for nature and the weak:
themes.description: In Chapter 6, Adam and Eve were going to protect nature and help the weak. Connect this with small actions for nature and for people who need help today.

themes.title: Calm instead of harm:
themes.description: In Chapter 9, Habil says, “I won’t fight back or harm you.” Discuss peaceful ways to solve problems at school and online.

actions: Make a class poster “Different and equal” with one respectful sentence from every learner.
Plan one small action for nature at school (watering plants, collecting litter) and write two “to + verb” sentences about why you do it.
Write three class rules for solving problems calmly with “We won’t …” and “We should …”.

exitTicket: One thing that happened in today’s chapter, and the sentence that shows it: …
One language pattern I looked at today, and what it does: …
One thing I can do this week that shows a value from the chapter: …

miniProject.title: Lessons from the First Family
miniProject.desc: In groups, choose one lesson from the book: Respect for difference (Chapter 1), useful knowledge (Chapter 3), learning from a mistake (Chapter 5), giving your best (Chapter 8) or controlling anger (Chapters 9–10). Make a simple poster or a one-minute audio clip in English: Copy one sentence from the book, explain it in your own words and give two examples from school life. Use at least two Language Focus patterns, for example “should”, “told … not to” or “decided never to”.

reflectivePrompt.title: A Mistake and a New Decision
reflectivePrompt.desc: In Chapter 5, Adam and Eve made a mistake, said sorry to Allah, learned from their mistake and decided never to repeat it. Write four to six short sentences about a small mistake you made at school or at home. What happened? Was it on purpose? What did you learn, and what did you decide?

valuesEducation.title: TYMM Values in Action
valuesEducation.description: Use only values the chapter really supports. Learners find the story evidence first, then connect the value to a small, observable action at school or at home. See https://tymm.meb.gov.tr/beceriler/erdem-deger-eylem-cercevesi.

items.label: D14 Respect
items.value: Respect is practised through non-ranking language about difference and polite disagreement.

items.label: D16 Responsibility
items.value: Responsibility becomes visible through the chapter’s jobs: growing crops, keeping animals, building, protecting nature and helping the weak.

items.label: D6 Honesty / D10 Humility
items.value: Admitting a mistake, saying sorry and rejecting arrogance are linked to concrete choices in Chapters 3 and 5.

items.label: D5 Sensitivity / D20 Helpfulness
items.value: Care and helpfulness are connected to protecting nature, helping the weak and giving one’s best.

items.label: D12 Patience / D9 Compassion
items.value: Controlling anger, refusing to harm and asking for help are explored calmly through Chapters 9–10.

questions: Which sentence in the story shows this value?
What small action could show the same value at school or at home?
Which part is story evidence and which part is your own application?

cefrProfile.intro: This book is written for CEFR A2. The table links the A2 descriptors of the End-of-Level Test A2 to the chapters of this book where learners practise them.

rows.descriptor: Can understand short, simple texts containing the highest frequency vocabulary, including a proportion of shared international vocabulary items.
practice: Chapter 4 (Paradise and the Warning): Find why Allah gave Adam a wife (So, …).
Chapter 8 (Story of Habil and Qabil): Fill the three-row grid for Habil and Qabil with words from the text.
Whole book: Knowledge Check and Final Challenge.

rows.descriptor: Can find specific, predictable information in simple everyday material such as advertisements, prospectuses, menus, reference lists and timetables.
practice: Chapter 8 (Story of Habil and Qabil): Fill the three-row grid for Habil and Qabil with words from the text.
Whole book: the journey map and the Places & People cards.

rows.descriptor: Can write a series of simple phrases and sentences linked with simple connectors like “and”, “but” and “because”.
practice: Chapter 8 (Story of Habil and Qabil): Use: “Giving my best” think-pair-share, each learner thinks of a time they had to do something and gave their best (a present, a project, help at home), writes three sentences and tells a partner.

Chapter 9 (The First Crime): Use: “Stop and ask” in pairs, learners choose a safe everyday problem (a lost bag, an argument in a game) and write four sentences (I won’t … / I became … / I don’t know what I should do. / My teacher showed me …)
Language Review, “Use: A Plan That Changed”: Write 4–5 sentences about a changed plan. Tell a partner first.

rows.descriptor: Can give a simple description or presentation of people, living or working conditions, daily routines, likes/dislikes, etc. as a short series of simple phrases and sentences linked into a list.
practice: Chapter 5 (Satan’s Lie and Regret): Describe a small mistake at school or at home and one responsible next step (say sorry, fix it, decide something new).
Chapter 8 (Story of Habil and Qabil): Describe one situation where you give your best, and label it clearly as your own example.
Language Review, “Use: A Plan That Changed”: Write 4–5 sentences about a changed plan. Tell a partner first.

test.title: End-of-Level Test A2
test.when: Give the test when the class has finished the A2 books it reads this term. It has four parts and takes about 60 minutes plus a short speaking test for each learner.
parts: Reading and Language (40 minutes): in the app. The learner gets a test code at the end.
Writing (20 minutes): on paper. Write an email to a friend about a visit to an old place. (50–70 words)
Speaking (about 6 minutes): one learner with the teacher, in 2 parts.
Scoring: type the test code in “Score a test”, then score Writing and Speaking with the bands. Copy the pilot line for the pilot results sheet.

professionalDevelopment.intro: Use these steps to plan your own development with this book: rate yourself on the EPG areas with this book’s chapters, let a colleague observe one of two lessons, keep a short log after each chapter, run one small classroom enquiry, work with colleagues, and agree on scoring before the End-of-Level Test.

peerObservation.focus: Say what Iblis claimed about himself and why (fire and soil).
lookFor: Instruction: Read the six sentences on the board with your partner. Is it Iblis’s idea, or is it true in the story? Write each sentence in the right column.
Check questions: How many columns are there? (two) / What do you say in the class check? (the clue word)

While learners work: Listen for the clue words “believed” and “thought” in pairs that sort correctly. A pair that puts “fire is better than clay” under “true” needs the question “Who says this?”. Note two good clue words to praise in the class check.
Evidence of “Idea vs chapter message”: Sorts all six sentences and names a clue word such as believed.

peerObservation.focus: Say what Adam taught people and what Adam and Eve taught their children.
lookFor: Instruction: Draw three boxes with your partner: for many years, Then, After the death of Adam. Copy one sentence from the story into each box.
Check questions: How many boxes? (three) / Where do you write Adam’s teachings? (under his box)

While learners work: Check that the teachings under Adam’s box are from the text: be honest, do good, stop bad, remember Allah. In the Use task, listen for “warn us against”. Collect two good sentences on the board for the class.
Evidence of “Teachings from the text”: Lists only the teachings in the text.

reflectionLog: After each chapter, answer the chapter’s “After the lesson” question in one or two sentences.
Write down the rubric criterion that most learners had not yet reached and the support you gave.
Every three or four chapters, look at the grammar sequence of this book and plan one short recycling activity for a form learners still avoid.
Before the End-of-Level Test, read your notes and choose two chapters to revise with the class.
standardisation: Before scoring, read the A2 descriptors for written and spoken production in the CEFR table of this book.

With a colleague, score the same three writing papers on your own with the A2 writing bands (Task, Organisation, Grammar, Vocabulary). Then compare and talk about any criterion where your scores differ by more than one band.
Score one speaking test together in the same way: both listen, both score, then compare.
Keep one agreed paper for each band as a sample for later scoring.

selfAssessment.prompt: Chapter 2: Could learners do this by the end of the lesson: “Explain what Adam could do and why he was wiser, using the chapter’s reason”? Which stage of the lesson flow helped most, and which did not?
Chapter 4 is planned for 40 minutes. Which stage took longer than planned, and what did you move to the next lesson?
Before the pair or group work in Chapter 5, did you ask “Where do the five steps come from?” How many learners could answer before they started?
In Chapter 10, how many learners were secure on “Lesson ← event link”? What did you do for those who were not yet secure?

When you asked “What do people grow or raise near your town (wheat in Konya, hazelnuts on the Black Sea)?” in Chapter 6, did learners describe other cultures with facts or with stereotypes? Which words did you give them?

Which of the likely errors listed for Chapter 8 did you hear (*Habil was a kind · *Qabil was farmer · *loved take care · *must to offer · *goodest, *most healthy)? Did you correct them during the activity or after it, and why?
Which app tools did your learners use with this book (audio, Word Notes, the exercises and their result codes)? Which one gave you the most useful information about their learning?
Read your reflection log for this book. What is one change you will make the next time you teach this book, and who will you share it with?

actionResearch.question: Do my learners still use could + base verb for past ability correctly after Chapter 2, or do they go back to *could to swim / *could swam?
steps: Baseline: in the Chapter 2 Use task, count how many learners write could + base verb correctly about Adam.
Recycle: in Chapters 7 and 10, ask each learner for one sentence about what a person in the story could or could not do, and count again.
Check: after the A2 End-of-Level Test, open Score a test for each code and note item 20 (could for past ability). Count correct answers in the class.
Decide: compare the three counts and write one change you will make in Chapter 2 next time.

collaboration: Share your counts for could for past ability with another English teacher who uses this book, and agree on one activity to try in both classes.
Plan the Chapter 1 respect discussion (soil and skin colors) with the class guidance teacher, so the class rule you agree is followed outside English lessons too.

objectives: I can say what Allah created Adam (pbuh) from.
I can say why people have different skin colors.
I can use past forms and “was going to”.
content.pedagogy: Look, listen and read first. Then find the answer sentences, do the Quick Challenge, and use the chapter’s Language Focus.
content.grammarFocus: Match verbs with their past forms (say → said, begin → began, get → got). Choose collected, was going to and shaped. Then complete lines with because, After that and Because of this. Remember: He was going to, not He were going to.
content.pronunciationFocus: Say the stress: MES-sen-ger, cu-ri-OS-i-ty, GRAND-chil-dren. The -ed in created is an extra part: cre-A-ted. Say “Because of this” as one group.
content.lessonPlan: Look at the title and the picture. What can you see in the sky and on the earth? Listen to the chapter once. Follow the text with your eyes. Read paragraph 3 again. Where did the soil come from?
discussionPoints: We are all children of Adam (pbuh), with many skin colors. How can you show respect to a person who looks different from you?
interactiveTips: Tap the picture hotspots “Soil” and “The Sky and the Earth”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Go back to paragraph 3. Find the words “Because of this” and read the sentence before them again. Try again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Retell the start of the story in three or four short sentences. Use past forms like created and collected, one was going to sentence, and After that or Then.

whatToNotice: First the chapter tells us what happened. Then it tells us Allah’s plan for the first human.
Look at “He told the angels that He was going to create a human.” was going to shows a plan for later.
readListen: Look at the title and the picture. What can you see in the sky and on the earth?
Listen to the chapter once. Follow the text with your eyes.
Read paragraph 3 again. Where did the soil come from?
Tap the picture hotspots “Soil” and “The Sky and the Earth”.
findAnswerInStory: Paragraph 1: find who Adam (pbuh) is and what Allah created him from.
Paragraph 2: find what the angels did when they heard the news.
Paragraph 4: find the four colors of the children of Adam (pbuh).
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: messenger, soil, curiosity, grandchildren.
“They began waiting with curiosity.” Did the angels want to know more? Say yes or no.
Write one sentence with grandchildren: “My grandmother has … grandchildren.”
content.quickChallengeGuide: The question asks why people’s skin colors are not all the same. Read paragraph 3 before you choose.
wrongAnswerSupport: Go back to paragraph 3.
Find the words “Because of this” and read the sentence before them again.
Try again.
selfCheck: Can I say what Allah created Adam (pbuh) from?
Can I say why humans have different skin colors?
Can I say “He was going to …” correctly?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Retell the start of the story in three or four short sentences. Use past forms like created and collected, one was going to sentence, and After that or Then.
content.reflectionPrompt: We are all children of Adam (pbuh), with many skin colors. How can you show respect to a person who looks different from you?

objectives: I can say why Adam (pbuh) was wiser than the angels.
I can say what the angels thought and what Iblis thought.
I can use could, wiser than and thought.
content.pedagogy: Look, listen and read first. Then find the answer sentences, do the Quick Challenge, and use the chapter’s Language Focus.
content.grammarFocus: Decide what could means in “Adam could learn and understand.” Complete lines with wiser, to and more. Then build the sentence “Iblis thought Adam was an unimportant creature created from clay.” We say wiser than, not wisest than.
content.pronunciationFocus: Say the stress: KNOW-ledge, re-SPECT, ad-MIRED. The k in knowledge is silent. Say “wiser than the angels” as one group.
content.lessonPlan: Look at the title. What do knowledge and respect mean to you? Listen to the chapter once. Follow the text with your eyes. Read paragraph 2 again. Find the word But.
discussionPoints: The angels respected Adam, but Iblis did not. How can you show respect to someone who knows more than you?
interactiveTips: Tap the picture hotspots “Knowledge” and “The Angels”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Go back to paragraph 1. Find the word because and read what comes after it. Try again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Write or say three or four short sentences about Adam and the two views. Use could, one comparison with than, because and but.

whatToNotice: The angels and Iblis looked at Adam in two very different ways.
Look at “Adam could learn and understand.” could tells us what he was able to do.
readListen: Look at the title. What do knowledge and respect mean to you?
Listen to the chapter once. Follow the text with your eyes.
Read paragraph 2 again. Find the word But.
Tap the picture hotspots “Knowledge” and “The Angels”.
findAnswerInStory: Paragraph 1: find what Allah told the angels to do.
Paragraph 1: find two things Allah gave Adam or taught him.
Paragraph 2: find what the angels thought and what Iblis thought.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: respect, knowledge, admired, clay.
“They all admired him and respected him.” Did the angels like Adam? Say yes or no.
Write one sentence: “I admire … because …”
content.quickChallengeGuide: The question asks why Adam knew more than the angels. Read paragraph 1 before you choose.
wrongAnswerSupport: Go back to paragraph 1.
Find the word because and read what comes after it.
Try again.
selfCheck: Can I say what Adam (pbuh) could do?
Can I say how the angels and Iblis thought about Adam?
Can I say “… is wiser than …” correctly?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Write or say three or four short sentences about Adam and the two views. Use could, one comparison with than, because and but.
content.reflectionPrompt: The angels respected Adam, but Iblis did not. How can you show respect to someone who knows more than you?

objectives: I can say why Iblis thought he was better than Adam.
I can tell what Iblis thought from what is true in the chapter.
I can use better than, more valuable and couldn’t.
content.pedagogy: Look, listen and read first. Then find the answer sentences, do the Quick Challenge, and use the chapter’s Language Focus.
content.grammarFocus: Sort parts into “What Iblis thought” and “What the chapter says is true”. Choose better, more valuable and couldn’t. Then complete lines with But and because. We say better than, not gooder than.
content.pronunciationFocus: Say the stress: AR-ro-gant, VAL-u-a-ble, CREA-ture, OR-i-gin. Make fire and soil strong: You created me from FIRE, and You created Adam from SOIL.
content.lessonPlan: Look at the title. Check the Word Note for arrogant. Listen to the chapter once. Follow the text with your eyes. Read paragraph 3 again. What makes people great?
discussionPoints: Where we come from does not make us better. Useful knowledge helps us do good. What is one useful thing you can learn and use to help others?
interactiveTips: Tap the picture hotspots “Fire and Soil” and “I Am Better”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Paragraph 1 has Iblis’s words. Read them again. Paragraph 2 is about Adam’s knowledge. Paragraph 3 is about clay, fire and useful knowledge. Match again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Write or say three or four short sentences about Iblis’s wrong idea. Use Iblis thought …, one comparison, But … and because.

whatToNotice: Iblis only looked at fire and soil. The chapter says something else makes people great.
Look at “He thought little and was wrong about Adam.” The chapter tells us Iblis’s idea was wrong.
readListen: Look at the title. Check the Word Note for arrogant.
Listen to the chapter once. Follow the text with your eyes.
Read paragraph 3 again. What makes people great?
Tap the picture hotspots “Fire and Soil” and “I Am Better”.
findAnswerInStory: Paragraph 1: find Iblis’s answer to Allah’s question.
Paragraph 2: find what made Adam more valuable.
Paragraph 4: find what Allah said to Iblis.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: arrogant, valuable, creature, origin.
“believed his origin was better”: origin is where you come from. What was Iblis’s origin?
Write one sentence: “… is valuable to me because …”
content.quickChallengeGuide: You will match four parts: Iblis, Adam, clay or fire, and useful knowledge. The answers are in paragraphs 1, 2 and 3.
wrongAnswerSupport: Paragraph 1 has Iblis’s words. Read them again.
Paragraph 2 is about Adam’s knowledge. Paragraph 3 is about clay, fire and useful knowledge.
Match again.
selfCheck: Can I say what Iblis believed?
Can I say why his idea was wrong?
Can I say “… is more valuable than …” correctly?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Write or say three or four short sentences about Iblis’s wrong idea. Use Iblis thought …, one comparison, But … and because.
content.reflectionPrompt: Where we come from does not make us better. Useful knowledge helps us do good. What is one useful thing you can learn and use to help others?

objectives: I can say why Allah gave Adam (pbuh) a wife.
I can say the one warning in Paradise.
I can use “wanted … to”, “told … not to” and “started to”.
content.pedagogy: Look, listen and read first. Then find the answer sentences, do the Quick Challenge, and use the chapter’s Language Focus.
content.grammarFocus: Decide who Iblis wanted to lose Allah’s love. Choose to be, to be and not to. Then build “Then, Adam started to feel lonely in Paradise.” We say told them not to go, not told them to not go.
content.pronunciationFocus: Say the stress: LONE-ly, WON-der-ful, WARN-ing, im-AG-ine. Say “not to go near one tree” as one group.
content.lessonPlan: Look at the picture. Can you find the one tree? Listen to the chapter once. Follow the text with your eyes. Read paragraph 2 again. Find the word So.
discussionPoints: Allah gave Adam and Eve many gifts and only one warning. Why is it important to listen to a warning?
interactiveTips: Tap the picture hotspots “Eve (Hawwa)” and “The One Tree”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Go back to paragraph 2. Find the word So and read the sentence before it again. Try again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Write or say three or four short sentences about a safe warning, for example near a busy road. Use one wanted … to sentence, one started to sentence, and told … to or told … not to.

whatToNotice: The chapter has two parts: Iblis’s anger, then Adam and Eve in Paradise.
Look at “He told Adam and Eve not to go near one tree.” not to shows what they must not do.
readListen: Look at the picture. Can you find the one tree?
Listen to the chapter once. Follow the text with your eyes.
Read paragraph 2 again. Find the word So.
Tap the picture hotspots “Eve (Hawwa)” and “The One Tree”.
findAnswerInStory: Paragraph 1: find two things Iblis wanted or did not want.
Paragraph 1: find what Allah told Adam about Iblis.
Paragraph 2: find how Adam felt and what Allah gave him.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: lonely, wonderful, warning, imagine.
“Adam started to feel lonely in Paradise.” Was Adam happy or sad?
Write one sentence with imagine: “I can imagine …”
content.quickChallengeGuide: The question asks why Allah gave Adam a wife. Read paragraph 2 before you choose.
wrongAnswerSupport: Go back to paragraph 2.
Find the word So and read the sentence before it again.
Try again.
selfCheck: Can I say how Adam felt before Eve came?
Can I say Allah’s one warning?
Can I say “He told them not to …” correctly?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Write or say three or four short sentences about a safe warning, for example near a busy road. Use one wanted … to sentence, one started to sentence, and told … to or told … not to.
content.reflectionPrompt: Allah gave Adam and Eve many gifts and only one warning. Why is it important to listen to a warning?

objectives: I can say what Iblis’s lie was.
I can say what Adam (pbuh) and Eve did after their mistake.
I can use “If …, you will …” and “decided never to”.
content.pedagogy: Look, listen and read first. Then find the answer sentences, do the Quick Challenge, and use the chapter’s Language Focus.
content.grammarFocus: Decide what the If part and the will part mean in Iblis’s words. Choose forgot, made and to repeat. Then match phrases like After a while and banned. We say make a mistake, not do a mistake.
content.pronunciationFocus: Say the stress: mis-TAKE, for-GET-ful, su-PE-ri-or. Stop for a moment after the comma in “If you eat from that one tree, you will never die.”
content.lessonPlan: Look at the title. What is a lie? Listen to the chapter once. Follow the text with your eyes. Read paragraph 3 again. Find four things Adam and Eve did after the mistake.
discussionPoints: Adam and Eve said sorry and learned. Iblis never said he was wrong. What can you do after you make a mistake?
interactiveTips: Tap the picture hotspots “The Lie” and “The Mistake”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Read the chapter again from the start. Stop after each paragraph and say what happened. Put the events in that order. Try again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Write or say four short sentences about a small mistake, like forgetting a friend’s birthday. Use I made a mistake, it wasn’t on purpose, I learned … and I decided never to ….

whatToNotice: After a mistake, Adam and Eve and Iblis did very different things.
Look at “They made a mistake, but it wasn’t on purpose.” They did not plan the mistake.
readListen: Look at the title. What is a lie?
Listen to the chapter once. Follow the text with your eyes.
Read paragraph 3 again. Find four things Adam and Eve did after the mistake.
Tap the picture hotspots “The Lie” and “The Mistake”.
findAnswerInStory: Paragraph 1: find what Iblis said about the tree.
Paragraph 2: find what Adam and Eve forgot.
Paragraph 4: find what Iblis believed about himself.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: lie, mistake, forgetful, superior.
“It was a big lie.” Was Iblis really their friend? Say yes or no.
Write one sentence: “I made a mistake when …, and I learned …”
content.quickChallengeGuide: You will put four events in order. The events go in the same order as paragraphs 1, 2 and 3.
wrongAnswerSupport: Read the chapter again from the start.
Stop after each paragraph and say what happened.
Put the events in that order. Try again.
selfCheck: Can I say Iblis’s lie?
Can I say two things Adam and Eve did after the mistake?
Can I say “They decided never to …” correctly?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Write or say four short sentences about a small mistake, like forgetting a friend’s birthday. Use I made a mistake, it wasn’t on purpose, I learned … and I decided never to ….
content.reflectionPrompt: Adam and Eve said sorry and learned. Iblis never said he was wrong. What can you do after you make a mistake?

objectives: I can say where Adam (pbuh) and Eve lived after Paradise.
I can say three jobs they were going to do on earth.
I can use “were going to”, to + verb and not to.
content.pedagogy: Look, listen and read first. Then find the answer sentences, do the Quick Challenge, and use the chapter’s Language Focus.
content.grammarFocus: Decide what were going to means here: Work for the future, not walking to a place. Build “They were going to build houses, protect nature and help the weak.” Then choose to, to and not to. We say on earth to live there, not for live there.
content.pronunciationFocus: Say the stress: PLAN-et, pro-TECT, NA-ture. Stop a little at each comma: Build houses, / protect nature / and help the weak.
content.lessonPlan: Look at the picture. What work can you see on the land? Listen to the chapter once. Follow the text with your eyes. Read paragraph 1 again. Find the verbs after “They were going to”.
discussionPoints: Adam and Eve were going to protect nature and help the weak. What is one thing you can do this week for nature or for a person who needs help?
interactiveTips: Tap the picture hotspots “A New Home” and “Work on the Land”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Go back to the last paragraph. Find the word followed and read that sentence again. Ask yourself: Did Iblis stay far away? Then try again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Write or say four short sentences about a useful job, like caring for a garden. Say your plan with going to, give a reason with to + verb, and say one thing you want people to do or not to do.

whatToNotice: Adam and Eve had a big job on earth. Iblis was there too.
Look at “He was still around.” still means Iblis did not go away.
readListen: Look at the picture. What work can you see on the land?
Listen to the chapter once. Follow the text with your eyes.
Read paragraph 1 again. Find the verbs after “They were going to”.
Tap the picture hotspots “A New Home” and “Work on the Land”.
findAnswerInStory: Paragraph 1: find what Allah did first.
Paragraph 1: find two things they used land for.
Paragraph 2: find what Iblis wanted.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: crops, rule, nature, weak.
“help the weak”: Do weak people need help? Say yes or no.
Write one sentence: “I can help … because …”
content.quickChallengeGuide: The sentence is about Iblis on earth. Read the last paragraph before you decide.
wrongAnswerSupport: Go back to the last paragraph.
Find the word followed and read that sentence again.
Ask yourself: Did Iblis stay far away? Then try again.
selfCheck: Can I say two things Adam and Eve were going to do?
Can I say what Iblis wanted?
Can I use to + verb to give a reason?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Write or say four short sentences about a useful job, like caring for a garden. Say your plan with going to, give a reason with to + verb, and say one thing you want people to do or not to do.
content.reflectionPrompt: Adam and Eve were going to protect nature and help the weak. What is one thing you can do this week for nature or for a person who needs help?

objectives: I can say what Adam (pbuh) taught people.
I can say why Adam and Eve warned their children against Iblis.
I can use “teach … to”, “warn … against”, Then and After.
content.pedagogy: Look, listen and read first. Then find the answer sentences, do the Quick Challenge, and use the chapter’s Language Focus.
content.grammarFocus: Choose to, against and not. Match phrases like for many years and took the same way. Then put five sentences in order with Then and After. We say warn someone against a danger.
content.pronunciationFocus: Say the stress: HON-est (the h is silent), be-HAVE, EN-e-my. Say the list slowly: Be honest, / do good, / stop bad.
content.lessonPlan: Look at the title. Who was the first Messenger? Listen to the chapter once. Follow the text with your eyes. Read paragraph 1 again. Find four things Adam taught people.
discussionPoints: Adam taught people to be honest and to remember Allah. What is one good thing you can teach a friend or a family member?
interactiveTips: Tap the picture hotspots “Chosen by Allah” and “Teaching”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Go back to paragraph 2. Find the word because after “warned their children” and read that sentence again. Try again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Write or say four short sentences of good advice for a friend or a family member. Use I teach … to …, I warn … against …, because and not ….

whatToNotice: The chapter moves from Adam’s life to the messengers who came after him.
Look at “Iblis was their enemy, not their friend.” not shows which idea is wrong.
readListen: Look at the title. Who was the first Messenger?
Listen to the chapter once. Follow the text with your eyes.
Read paragraph 1 again. Find four things Adam taught people.
Tap the picture hotspots “Chosen by Allah” and “Teaching”.
findAnswerInStory: Paragraph 1: find what Allah made Adam.
Paragraph 2: find what Adam and Eve taught their children.
Paragraph 3: find what happened after the death of Adam (pbuh).
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: honest, behave, enemy, peace.
“Some days brought them peace”: Were those days calm or difficult?
Write one sentence: “An honest person …”
content.quickChallengeGuide: The question asks why Adam and Eve warned their children against Iblis. Read paragraph 2 before you choose.
wrongAnswerSupport: Go back to paragraph 2.
Find the word because after “warned their children” and read that sentence again.
Try again.
selfCheck: Can I say two things Adam taught people?
Can I say why Iblis was not their friend?
Can I say “They taught … to …” correctly?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Write or say four short sentences of good advice for a friend or a family member. Use I teach … to …, I warn … against …, because and not ….
content.reflectionPrompt: Adam taught people to be honest and to remember Allah. What is one good thing you can teach a friend or a family member?

content.chapter: Chapter 8: Story of Habil and Qabil
objectives: I can say how Habil and Qabil were different.
I can say what each brother gave to Allah.
I can use was + adjective, had to and the best.
content.pedagogy: Look, listen and read first. Then find the answer sentences, do the Quick Challenge, and use the chapter’s Language Focus.
content.grammarFocus: Sort parts into “What the person was like” and “The person’s job”. Choose taking, had to and best and healthiest. Then complete the line with but. We say loved taking care, not loved take care.
content.pronunciationFocus: Say the stress: SHEP-herd (the h is silent), FARM-er, OF-fer-ing, JEAL-ous. Make the two names strong: HABIL brought … but QABIL brought ….
content.lessonPlan: Look at the picture. Who is the shepherd and who is the farmer? Listen to the chapter once. Follow the text with your eyes. Read paragraph 2 again. Find the word but between the two gifts.
discussionPoints: Habil gave his best. What is one thing you can do with your best effort this week?
interactiveTips: Tap the picture hotspots “Habil the Shepherd” and “Qabil the Farmer”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Go back to paragraph 1 and find became and was a. Then go to paragraph 2 and find brought. Match again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Write or say four short sentences about a good choice you made. Say what you are like, one thing you had to do, why you did it, and how you gave your best.

whatToNotice: The two brothers were different in who they were, in their work and in their gifts.
Look at “Real goodness is giving the best and the most loved.” This is the lesson of the chapter.
readListen: Look at the picture. Who is the shepherd and who is the farmer?
Listen to the chapter once. Follow the text with your eyes.
Read paragraph 2 again. Find the word but between the two gifts.
Tap the picture hotspots “Habil the Shepherd” and “Qabil the Farmer”.
findAnswerInStory: Paragraph 1: find two words about Habil and one word about Qabil.
Paragraph 1: find each brother’s job.
Paragraph 2: find what each brother brought.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: shepherd, farmer, offering, jealous.
“Qabil was mostly jealous.” Was he happy when other people had good things?
Write one sentence: “My best gift to … was …”
content.quickChallengeGuide: You will match each brother’s work and each brother’s offering. The jobs are in paragraph 1 and the offerings are in paragraph 2.
wrongAnswerSupport: Go back to paragraph 1 and find became and was a.
Then go to paragraph 2 and find brought.
Match again.
selfCheck: Can I say each brother’s job?
Can I say how the two gifts were different?
Can I say “They had to …” correctly?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Write or say four short sentences about a good choice you made. Say what you are like, one thing you had to do, why you did it, and how you gave your best.
content.reflectionPrompt: Habil gave his best. What is one thing you can do with your best effort this week?

objectives: I can say what Habil answered his angry brother.
I can say what the crow did.
I can use won’t, became and “I don’t know what I should do”.
content.pedagogy: Look, listen and read first. Then find the answer sentences, do the Quick Challenge, and use the chapter’s Language Focus.
content.grammarFocus: Decide what won’t shows in Habil’s words. Match phrases like Qabil was not angry anymore. Then choose became, should and sent. We say became and sent, not becomed and sended.
content.pronunciationFocus: Say won’t with a long o: It is not want. Say the stress: PAN-ic, DIG-ging. Say Habil’s words in a calm voice: “You are my brother, and I fear Allah.”
content.lessonPlan: Look at the title. This chapter is sad, so take your time. Listen to the chapter once. Follow the text with your eyes. Read Habil’s words in quotation marks (“ ”) again.
discussionPoints: Habil said no to fighting. What can you do when you feel very angry? Who can you talk to?
interactiveTips: Tap the picture hotspots “The Crow” and “Panic”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Go back to paragraph 1. Find “I won’t fight back or harm you.” and read the next sentence. Try again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Write or say four short sentences about a safe problem, like a lost key. Use I won’t …, I became …, I don’t know what I should do, and someone showed me how to ….

whatToNotice: This chapter is sad. Anger made Qabil do the worst thing, but Habil chose not to fight.
Look at “Qabil was not angry anymore, and he felt so sad.” His feeling changed.
readListen: Look at the title. This chapter is sad, so take your time.
Listen to the chapter once. Follow the text with your eyes.
Read Habil’s words in quotation marks (“ ”) again.
Tap the picture hotspots “The Crow” and “Panic”.
findAnswerInStory: Paragraph 1: find why Allah was pleased with Habil’s offering.
Paragraph 1: find Habil’s answer to his brother.
Paragraph 2: find what the crow did.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: crow, panic, digging, harm.
“I won’t fight back or harm you.” Did Habil want to hurt his brother?
Write one sentence: “When I feel afraid, I do not panic. I …”
content.quickChallengeGuide: The question asks why Habil said he would not fight back. Read Habil’s words in paragraph 1 before you choose.
wrongAnswerSupport: Go back to paragraph 1.
Find “I won’t fight back or harm you.” and read the next sentence.
Try again.
selfCheck: Can I say Habil’s answer?
Can I say how Qabil’s feelings changed?
Can I say “I don’t know what I should do” correctly?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Write or say four short sentences about a safe problem, like a lost key. Use I won’t …, I became …, I don’t know what I should do, and someone showed me how to ….
content.reflectionPrompt: Habil said no to fighting. What can you do when you feel very angry? Who can you talk to?

objectives: I can say why Adam (pbuh) was very sad.
I can say how Adam’s message went around the world.
I can use should, had to and still.
content.pedagogy: Look, listen and read first. Then find the answer sentences, do the Quick Challenge, and use the chapter’s Language Focus.
content.grammarFocus: Match verbs with their past forms (go → went, lose → lost, take → took). Choose should, had to and still. Then build “It tells them to be well-behaved and kind to others.” We say should stay, not should to stay.
content.pronunciationFocus: Say the stress: con-TROL, ad-VI-ses, world-WIDE, MES-sage. The -es in advises is an extra part: ad-VI-ses.
content.lessonPlan: Look at the title. What do you remember about Adam (pbuh)? Listen to the chapter once. Follow the text with your eyes. Read paragraph 1 again. Find the lesson with should.
discussionPoints: The story tells us to stay away from jealousy and to control our anger. Which one will you work on this week?

metadata.title: Prophet Adam A2 — Self-Study Guide
metadata.subtitle: Look • Listen • Read • Check • Use
metadata.estimatedStudyTime: About 20 minutes per chapter, plus the review pages at the end
metadata.whoIsThisFor: A2 learners who study the story of Prophet Adam at home or on their own.
learningGoals: Understand the 10 chapters of the story of Prophet Adam (pbuh).
Find the answer sentence in the story.
Learn the Word Notes of each chapter.
Use each chapter’s Language Focus in your own sentences.
Turn respect, humility and self-control into small actions.
recommendedUse: Study one chapter at a time.
Answer the Quick Challenge before you read the feedback.
Do the Language Focus after you understand the chapter.
Do the review pages after Chapter 10.

sections.title: 1. One Chapter at a Time
sections.text: Study one chapter in one sitting. It takes about 20 minutes. Open “Study Path” to see the steps for your chapter.
points: Look at the title and the picture.
Listen and follow the text.
Read one paragraph at a time.
Do the Quick Challenge.
Do the Language Focus.

sections.title: 2. Listen and Read
sections.text: Every chapter has audio. Listen first, then read.
points: First time: Listen for the main idea.
Second time: Follow the words with your eyes.
Stop the audio and say one short sentence again.

sections.title: 3. Word Notes and Hotspots
sections.text: Each chapter has four underlined words. Tap a word to see its Word Note. Tap the hotspots on the picture for short notes.
points: Read the word in its sentence first.
Guess the meaning, then check the Word Note.
Write the word and one sentence in your notebook.

sections.title: 4. Quick Challenge
sections.text: Each chapter has one Quick Challenge. Answer first, then read the feedback.
points: Wrong answer? Find the answer sentence.
Read it again.
Try again.

sections.title: 5. Language Focus
sections.text: Each chapter has four Language Focus activities. Do them after you understand the chapter. They use sentences from the story.
points: Activity 1: look at a story sentence and its meaning.
Activities 2 and 3: practise the words and forms.
Last activity: Write or say three or four sentences of your own.

sections.title: 6. When It Is Hard
sections.text: It is fine to find a chapter hard. Change how you study, not your goal.
points: Listen to one paragraph only.
Read two or three lines at a time.
Look at the picture and the hotspots again.
Learn only two words today.

sections.title: 7. Values in the Story
sections.text: The story of Adam (pbuh) is about respect, humility, saying sorry, care and self-control. Turn each value into one small action.
points: Respect: All people are children of Adam, with many skin colors (Chapters 1 and 2).
Humility: Do not think you are better than others (Chapters 3 and 5).
Saying sorry: Learn from a mistake and do not repeat it (Chapter 5).
Care: Protect nature and help the weak (Chapter 6).
Giving your best: Give the best you have (Chapter 8).
Self-control: Stay calm when you are angry (Chapters 9 and 10).

sections.title: 8. At the End of the Book
sections.text: After Chapter 10, do the review pages in this order. Go back to a chapter when an answer is not clear.
